pages.title: Measure a pulse width and duty cycle
pages.text: Digital and pulse waveforms often need timing measurements in addition to frequency.
pages.sourceLesson: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

Period T is the interval between matching edges. Pulse width th is the duration the waveform spends high above a defined threshold. Duty cycle D = th/T × 100%. A 20% duty waveform is high one-fifth of each cycle, not necessarily one-fifth of its voltage amplitude. Rise time describes a specified percentage transition interval and can expose excessive capacitive loading or insufficient drive.
Limits and the technician’s decision
State the threshold used to define edge times; noise and ringing near the threshold can make an automatic measurement inconsistent.

worked.heading: Worked case · Measure a pulse width and duty cycle
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A pulse repeats every 5 ms and stays high for 1.5 ms.
Duty cycle = 1.5/5 = 0.30 or 30%; frequency = 1/0.005 = 200 Hz.
If a trace instead shows 0.3 ms high, D = 6%.

reflection.ask: A 2 kHz periodic pulse is high for 100 µs. What is its duty cycle?

pages.title: Choosing DMM, scope or spectrum measurement
pages.text: Measurement planning begins with the unknown behavior, not with the most impressive instrument on the bench.
pages.remember: The time-domain oscilloscope waveform at sufficient bandwidth and sample rate.
pages.sourceLesson: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

Use a DMM for stable numerical values with appropriate ranges. Use an oscilloscope for waveform shape, glitches, voltage/time relationships and edge behavior. A spectrum analyzer reports signal amplitude versus frequency, useful for harmonics, spurs and interference; it is not simply an oscilloscope with a different screen. A frequency counter measures repetition accurately under suitable input and signal-to-noise conditions. Choose the tool, expected result and reference connection before attaching anything.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Respect every input’s maximum voltage and RF power rating. A high-voltage transient can destroy a low-level spectrum input; use appropriate attenuators and isolation.

worked.heading: Worked case · Choosing DMM, scope or spectrum measurement
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A switching converter reads 5.0 V DC yet creates a 100 kHz ripple.
A scope can estimate its peak-to-peak ripple; a spectrum analyzer may show the switching fundamental and harmonics if its frequency span and input level are appropriate.
worked.conclusion: The time-domain oscilloscope waveform at sufficient bandwidth and sample rate.

reflection.ask: Which view best reveals whether a square wave has overshoot at each rising edge?
reflection.answer: The time-domain oscilloscope waveform at sufficient bandwidth and sample rate.

pages.title: Use a frequency sweep to study a circuit
pages.text: A frequency response is a set of paired input and output measurements, not a single gain number.
pages.sourceLesson: Turn time-domain measurements into filter and fault evidence

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

Hold the input amplitude and measurement method fixed, change frequency systematically, and record output magnitude and phase when needed. The voltage transfer magnitude is |H| = |Vout/Vin|; gain in decibels is 20 log10|H| when both voltages are compared at appropriate reference impedances. A log-frequency graph reveals behavior across decades without crowding high frequencies. A filter’s cutoff is tied to a specified response criterion such as −3 dB relative to the passband.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Take the input reading at each frequency too; a signal generator can change actual output due to source and load interactions.

worked.heading: Worked case · Use a frequency sweep to study a circuit
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: If Vin = 1 V RMS and Vout = 0.5 V RMS at one frequency, magnitude ratio = 0.5 and voltage gain ≈ −6.02 dB.
That is not the −3 dB cutoff point: −3 dB corresponds to an amplitude ratio of about 0.707.

reflection.ask: A response shows 0.707 Vout/Vin. Roughly what is its voltage gain?

pages.title: Units, logarithms and measurement graphs
pages.text: A properly labeled graph is part of technical reasoning, not decoration.
pages.remember: 10^(−20/20) = 0.1; output amplitude is one-tenth of input.
pages.sourceLesson: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

Keep units on both axes, note whether frequency is linear or logarithmic, and state what the decibel reference means. For a power ratio, gain_dB = 10 log10(Pout/Pin). For a voltage ratio across equal impedances or as a transfer magnitude, 20 log10(|Vout/Vin|) describes amplitude gain. These are not interchangeable in arbitrary impedance conditions. Metric prefixes matter: 10 kHz is 10,000 Hz; 10 µs is 0.000010 s. One missing prefix can misplace a filter knee by a decade or more.
Limits and the technician’s decision
When comparing measurements, also log source amplitude, channel coupling, attenuation, and load because changing any can imitate a circuit fault.

worked.heading: Worked case · Units, logarithms and measurement graphs
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A plot states “gain +6 dB.” If it is a voltage transfer between like measurement points, |Vout/Vin| ≈ 10^(6/20) ≈ 2.
If it is a power ratio, Pout/Pin ≈ 10^(6/10) ≈ 4.
worked.conclusion: 10^(−20/20) = 0.1; output amplitude is one-tenth of input.

reflection.ask: What is the voltage amplitude ratio corresponding to −20 dB?
reflection.answer: 10^(−20/20) = 0.1; output amplitude is one-tenth of input.

pages.title: A filter is a measured transfer behavior
pages.text: Calling a circuit low-pass or high-pass predicts a trend; a trustworthy report quantifies that trend.
pages.remember: Below its cutoff; at higher frequencies the capacitor diverts more signal toward the reference node.
pages.sourceLesson: Turn time-domain measurements into filter and fault evidence

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

An RC low-pass with its output across the capacitor generally passes slow variations and attenuates faster ones. Its ideal magnitude is |H| = 1/√(1+(f/fc)²), where fc = 1/(2πRC), under the stated unloaded model. A high-pass output across R instead suppresses slow/DC variation. Output loading, input impedance and component tolerances move the measured curve. A technician uses a small frequency sweep to compare a real response with the model.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Do not label a measured cutoff from one arbitrary low output reading; first establish passband and threshold conventions.

worked.heading: Worked case · A filter is a measured transfer behavior
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: For R = 1 kΩ and C = 100 nF, fc ≈ 1592 Hz.
At f = fc, ideal unloaded low-pass output is 0.707 × input (−3.01 dB).
If it is roughly half at 1.6 kHz, investigate loading or wrong component values.
worked.conclusion: Below its cutoff; at higher frequencies the capacitor diverts more signal toward the reference node.

reflection.ask: In an ideal RC low-pass, which frequency range passes most readily?
reflection.answer: Below its cutoff; at higher frequencies the capacitor diverts more signal toward the reference node.

pages.title: Time-domain and frequency-domain evidence agree
pages.text: A changing waveform is built from frequency components, so a filter can alter shape even when its fundamental frequency remains present.
pages.remember: It attenuates the higher harmonics that make an ideal square wave’s transitions sharp.
pages.sourceLesson: Turn time-domain measurements into filter and fault evidence

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

A square wave contains its fundamental and higher odd harmonics. Removing high-frequency harmonics rounds edges; an RC low-pass turns sharp transitions into approximately exponential changes. Conversely a high-pass responds strongly to edges while attenuating slow baseline changes. A scope reveals the shape; a spectrum view reveals which frequency components have changed. Both should fit the same circuit model.
Limits and the technician’s decision
A rounded output is not automatic proof of a defective gate: probe loading, output drive limits and the intended filter response can all cause it.

worked.heading: Worked case · Time-domain and frequency-domain evidence agree
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: Send a low-amplitude square wave through a simulated RC low-pass.
If its period is 1 ms but RC is 0.5 ms, the capacitor cannot fully charge/discharge within each half-cycle; the output becomes rounded and has smaller swing.
worked.conclusion: It attenuates the higher harmonics that make an ideal square wave’s transitions sharp.

reflection.ask: Why does a low-pass often round a square wave?
reflection.answer: It attenuates the higher harmonics that make an ideal square wave’s transitions sharp.

pages.title: Plan a defensible instrument characterization
pages.text: A good measurement record enables another person to repeat your test and get a comparable result.
pages.remember: For example: source amplitude/frequency method, probe and channel settings, load impedance; any three relevant recorded conditions.
pages.sourceLesson: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

Write the device under test, schematic and expected behavior first. Record equipment model, calibration/status if required, cable/probe configuration, voltage reference, load, stimulus shape/amplitude, sweep range, scale settings, and measured result with units. Change one variable at a time. Record unexpected behavior before adjusting controls so the evidence is not lost. Separate fact (“output dropped 20%”) from inference (“loading may be excessive”).
Limits and the technician’s decision
Written calculations and simulation qualify as conceptual practice, not a claim of independent hands-on scope competence.

worked.heading: Worked case · Plan a defensible instrument characterization
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A low-pass expected near 1.6 kHz appears to cut off near 160 Hz.
First check for 10× unit/setting errors: 100 nF versus 1 µF, 1 kΩ versus 10 kΩ, probe configuration, and generator output settings.
Then investigate genuine hardware variance.
worked.conclusion: For example: source amplitude/frequency method, probe and channel settings, load impedance; any three relevant recorded conditions.

reflection.ask: Name three setup conditions that must accompany a measured filter cutoff.
reflection.answer: For example: source amplitude/frequency method, probe and channel settings, load impedance; any three relevant recorded conditions.

examples.title: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

detail.problem: A 10 kΩ resistor charges a 10 µF capacitor from a 5 V step. Find τ and approximate voltage after one τ.
steps: After one τ, the capacitor has completed about 63% of the change.
After about 5τ = 0.5 s, it is near the final value.
detail.answer: τ = 0.1 s; Vc at one τ is about 3.15 V.
detail.transfer: A scope cursor can test both the predicted time and voltage on the charging curve.

examples.title: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

detail.problem: A 10 kOhm resistor charges a 100 uF capacitor from 0 V toward 5 V. Find tau and estimate voltage after one tau and five tau.
steps: After one tau, Vc≈0.632 x 5 V = 3.16 V.
After five tau, the capacitor is above 99% of the way to 5 V, roughly 4.97 V.
The current is initially 5/10k=0.5 mA and decreases as Vc rises.
detail.answer: tau=1 s; about 3.16 V at 1 s and approximately 5 V by 5 s.
detail.meaning: The time constant predicts the shape and timing of a real charging waveform.

examples.title: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

detail.problem: A waveform spans 4 vertical divisions at 0.5 V/div and one cycle spans 5 horizontal divisions at 200 µs/div.
steps: Vpp = 4 × 0.5 V = 2.0 V peak-to-peak.
Confirm the probe/channel attenuation setting before accepting amplitude.
detail.answer: 2.0 Vpp and 1 kHz.
detail.transfer: If the 10× probe is set to 10× but the channel assumes 1×, the amplitude display will be wrong even though the trace looks stable.

examples.title: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

detail.problem: A 3.3 V digital output appears as 0.33 V on the oscilloscope, while a DMM reads 3.29 V.
steps: The DMM suggests the node's DC level is near 3.3 V.
A factor-of-ten scope discrepancy strongly suggests probe attenuation mismatch: for example a 10x probe with the channel set to 1x, or vice versa.
Verify probe switch position and channel probe factor before changing the circuit.
Also verify the ground/reference point and DC coupling.
detail.answer: Check probe attenuation/configuration and reference before concluding the digital output is only 0.33 V.
detail.meaning: Instrument configuration is part of the measurement and can create a false fault symptom.

examples.title: Turn time-domain measurements into filter and fault evidence

detail.problem: An RC low-pass uses 1 kΩ and 0.1 µF. The measured cutoff is near 160 Hz, not the predicted value in your note of 1.6 kHz.
steps: A 160 Hz result suggests RC is about ten times larger.
Check whether the capacitor is 1.0 µF, the resistor is 10 kΩ, or a load adds effective impedance.
detail.answer: The tenfold mismatch points to a decade-value or effective-impedance error.
detail.transfer: Ratio and scale of error guide inspection more efficiently than replacing parts at random.

pages.title: A capacitor stores separated charge and electric-field energy
pages.text: Capacitance quantifies how much charge is stored per volt between conductive regions separated by an insulator.
pages.remember: Because E = ½CV²; for fixed C, energy is proportional to voltage squared.
pages.sourceLesson: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

Capacitance C = Q/V, in farads; a farad is a coulomb per volt. The dielectric and plate geometry determine C. A capacitor stores field energy E = ½CV², which explains why it can remain hazardous after supply power is removed. In the ideal model, i = C·dV/dt: current is needed to change voltage, and the voltage cannot jump instantly without unbounded current. Real components have leakage, equivalent series resistance (ESR) and voltage limits.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Treat capacitors as potentially charged even when the switch is off. Do not short unknown capacitors by hand or assume low capacitance means zero risk.

worked.heading: Worked case · A capacitor stores separated charge and electric-field energy
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A 100 µF capacitor held at 10 V stores E = 0.5 × 100×10⁻⁶ × 10² = 0.005 J = 5 mJ.
The same part at 20 V stores 20 mJ because energy scales with V².
worked.conclusion: Because E = ½CV²; for fixed C, energy is proportional to voltage squared.

reflection.ask: Why does doubling voltage quadruple stored capacitor energy?
reflection.answer: Because E = ½CV²; for fixed C, energy is proportional to voltage squared.

pages.title: Why capacitors do not pass steady DC through the dielectric
pages.text: A charging capacitor can produce current in the external wires even though charge does not cross an ideal dielectric.
pages.remember: No. It has decayed to about 0.7% of its initial value.
pages.sourceLesson: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

When a DC step is applied through a resistor, current initially flows while the plate charge changes. As the capacitor voltage approaches the supply, the resistor drop and current decrease. After sufficiently long steady conditions, ideal capacitor current approaches zero. A changing signal can keep changing the stored charge, which is why capacitors are used in coupling, bypass and filtering. The phrase “passes AC” is an informal shortcut; frequency, impedance and the connected circuit matter.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Do not treat a capacitor as an infinite-frequency short in every real circuit: leads, ESR, parasitic inductance and dielectric behavior limit that approximation.

worked.heading: Worked case · Why capacitors do not pass steady DC through the dielectric
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A 1 kΩ resistor and 100 µF capacitor have time constant τ = RC = 0.1 s.
From 0 V after one τ the capacitor rises to about 63% of a DC source; after three τ, about 95%.
worked.conclusion: No. It has decayed to about 0.7% of its initial value.

reflection.ask: After five RC time constants in an ideal charging circuit, is the current still near its initial value?
reflection.answer: No. It has decayed to about 0.7% of its initial value.

pages.title: Capacitor types, construction and polarity
pages.text: Two parts marked 10 µF may behave very differently because material, voltage rating and polarity vary.
pages.remember: Its effective capacitance can drop under DC voltage bias, depending on dielectric and package.
pages.sourceLesson: Component families, ratings, magnetism, and machines

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

Ceramic capacitors are compact and useful at high frequencies, but some classes lose significant effective capacitance under DC bias. Aluminum electrolytics offer comparatively large capacitance and may be polarized; reverse voltage can damage them. Film capacitors may be stable for timing and AC applications. Tantalum components have specific surge and polarity constraints. Select by actual capacitance under conditions, tolerance, working voltage, leakage, ESR, temperature and mechanical fit—not the nominal µF alone.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Do not reverse a polarized component; do not exceed working voltage. Source datasheets govern safe application and polarity markings.

worked.heading: Worked case · Capacitor types, construction and polarity
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A 10 µF 6.3 V ceramic capacitor on a 5 V rail may not provide 10 µF in operation, depending on dielectric and package.
Review its manufacturer DC-bias curve before using it as the only hold-up element.
worked.conclusion: Its effective capacitance can drop under DC voltage bias, depending on dielectric and package.

reflection.ask: Why might a ceramic marked 10 µF measure less while powered than on a benchtop meter?
reflection.answer: Its effective capacitance can drop under DC voltage bias, depending on dielectric and package.

pages.title: Inductance stores magnetic-field energy
pages.text: An inductor resists rapid change in current because current produces magnetic flux and flux change induces voltage.
pages.remember: Its current; instantaneous current change would require infinite voltage in the ideal relationship.
pages.sourceLesson: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

The ideal relationship is v = L·di/dt, where L is inductance in henries. In the ideal model current cannot jump instantaneously unless voltage is unbounded. An inductor stores E = ½LI²; it can create a high switching voltage when its current path is abruptly interrupted. Real coils have copper resistance, saturation limits, core loss and winding capacitance. At DC steady state an ideal inductor has zero voltage drop, but a real one still has resistive loss.
Limits and the technician’s decision
A relay coil or transformer winding can produce a switching transient. Never remove a current path without an appropriate rated suppression strategy.

worked.heading: Worked case · Inductance stores magnetic-field energy
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A 10 mH coil carrying 0.2 A stores E = ½ × 0.010 × (0.2)² = 0.0002 J, or 0.2 mJ.
If its current changes by 0.2 A over 1 ms, the ideal coil voltage magnitude is LΔI/Δt = 2 V.
worked.conclusion: Its current; instantaneous current change would require infinite voltage in the ideal relationship.

reflection.ask: Which variable is continuous in an ideal inductor across a switching instant?
reflection.answer: Its current; instantaneous current change would require infinite voltage in the ideal relationship.

pages.title: RL time constant and magnetic decay
pages.text: An inductive circuit has its own time scale, determined by inductance and the resistance through which current changes.
pages.remember: Time constant halves because τ = L/R.
pages.sourceLesson: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

For an ideal series RL step response, τ = L/R. After one τ, current in an energizing branch has reached about 63% of its final value; after one τ in a discharge, it has fallen to about 37% of its initial value. The energy drop is faster than current drop because E ∝ I². Real diode-clamped relay coils decay differently from a simple fixed-resistance RL circuit: the clamp changes voltage across the coil and thus the release speed.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Do not apply τ = L/R to a nonlinear snubber/diode without checking the actual current path and operating assumptions.

worked.heading: Worked case · RL time constant and magnetic decay
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: In an ideal exponential decay after 0.2 ms, current is ≈0.368 × its initial value.
worked.conclusion: Time constant halves because τ = L/R.

reflection.ask: What happens to ideal RL step response time when resistance doubles at fixed L?
reflection.answer: Time constant halves because τ = L/R.

pages.title: Coils, cores, coupling and saturation
pages.text: Inductors and transformers are physical windings whose magnetic surroundings determine more than the symbol suggests.
pages.remember: It does not establish allowable current, saturation behavior, copper loss, core loss or temperature limits.
pages.sourceLesson: Component families, ratings, magnetism, and machines

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

Adding turns generally increases inductance when geometry and material are held constant; a magnetic core can concentrate flux. A core saturates when additional magnetizing current yields little incremental flux, causing inductance to fall and current to rise rapidly. Lamination and ferrite materials reduce particular losses in appropriate frequency ranges. Nearby coils can couple through shared magnetic flux; mutual inductance is the basis for transformers.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Core selection is frequency-dependent; a mains-frequency laminated steel core is not a universal replacement for a high-frequency ferrite.

worked.heading: Worked case · Coils, cores, coupling and saturation
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: Two coils have equal nominal inductance but one is rated for 50 mA and another for 2 A before saturation.
At 0.5 A the first may no longer behave like the stated inductance.
Check the datasheet current rating and inductance-vs-current curve.
worked.conclusion: It does not establish allowable current, saturation behavior, copper loss, core loss or temperature limits.

reflection.ask: Why is a coil’s inductance rating alone insufficient for a power converter?
reflection.answer: It does not establish allowable current, saturation behavior, copper loss, core loss or temperature limits.

pages.title: Compare stored-field energy with dissipation
pages.text: Capacitors and inductors store and return energy; resistance turns energy into heat.
pages.remember: Energy; at fixed capacitance it scales with the square of voltage.
pages.sourceLesson: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

A capacitor’s stored energy E_C = ½CV² depends on voltage; an inductor’s E_L = ½LI² depends on current. In an ideal LC exchange, energy oscillates between electric and magnetic fields. Real series resistance and magnetic/dielectric losses cause damping. This is a useful bridge toward resonance and filters. A decibel measures a ratio, not an absolute stored energy, and should not be substituted into these physical energy equations.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Always distinguish instantaneous energy from average power and account for decay/loss pathways in practical devices.

worked.heading: Worked case · Compare stored-field energy with dissipation
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A 100 µF capacitor at 5 V stores 1.25 mJ; a 10 mH inductor at 0.5 A also stores 1.25 mJ.
Equal energy does not imply identical voltage, current or safe handling conditions.
worked.conclusion: Energy; at fixed capacitance it scales with the square of voltage.

reflection.ask: What kind of quantity does a capacitor store in its field, and what controls the amount?
reflection.answer: Energy; at fixed capacitance it scales with the square of voltage.

pages.title: How a step or square wave reveals reactive behavior
pages.text: Time-domain measurements show exactly what the differential relationships mean.
pages.remember: No. It moves only about 9.5% of the required step in an ideal first-order RC response.
pages.sourceLesson: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

Apply an ideal small step through a resistor to a capacitor: capacitor voltage ramps/exponentially approaches its new value rather than jumping. Apply a step to a simple RL branch: inductor current builds rather than instantly reaching V/R. With a square-wave stimulus, whether the branch reaches steady level depends on the half-period relative to τ. A transient response can therefore reveal an incorrect component decade.
Limits and the technician’s decision
A real oscilloscope and probe can add capacitance and alter the waveform. Build the model before attaching a probe and stay within protected low-voltage boundaries.

worked.heading: Worked case · How a step or square wave reveals reactive behavior
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: For RC with τ = 1 ms and a 2 kHz square wave, each half-cycle lasts 0.25 ms = 0.25τ.
The capacitor barely moves toward either rail before input polarity changes.
worked.conclusion: No. It moves only about 9.5% of the required step in an ideal first-order RC response.

reflection.ask: If the input holds a level for only 0.1τ, will a capacitor usually reach its final DC voltage?
reflection.answer: No. It moves only about 9.5% of the required step in an ideal first-order RC response.

pages.title: Capacitive and inductive reactance
pages.text: A field-storage component responds differently when the input changes faster.
pages.remember: Capacitive reactance halves; inductive reactance doubles.
pages.sourceLesson: From reactance to impedance, phase, and resonance

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

For sinusoidal steady state, X_C = 1/(2πfC) ohms and X_L = 2πfL ohms. Increasing frequency lowers ideal capacitive reactance but raises ideal inductive reactance. These quantities describe magnitude; their phase signs oppose each other. For a capacitor current leads voltage; for an inductor current lags voltage. You need this phase distinction before adding impedances in a network.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Reactance is calculated for a frequency, not measured with an ordinary DC ohmmeter. Real parts add resistance and parasitics.

worked.heading: Worked case · Capacitive and inductive reactance
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: At 1 kHz, a 100 nF capacitor has |X_C| ≈ 1592 Ω; a 10 mH inductor has X_L ≈ 62.8 Ω.
Neither is equivalent to the same fixed resistor at all frequencies.
worked.conclusion: Capacitive reactance halves; inductive reactance doubles.

reflection.ask: If the input frequency doubles, what happens to ideal X_C and X_L?
reflection.answer: Capacitive reactance halves; inductive reactance doubles.

goldTeaching.sectionNote: Use paper/simulation or approved protected low-voltage training only. Scope ground clips, inductive transients, charged capacitors, mains transformers and motor circuits create real hazards.

pages.title: Reactance and resistance are not the same quantity
pages.text: Both quantities may be expressed in ohms, but they describe different voltage-current relationships.
pages.remember: The capacitor introduces phase shift and stores/returns energy; the resistor ideally dissipates energy without reactive phase shift.
pages.sourceLesson: From reactance to impedance, phase, and resonance

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

Resistance dissipates power and, for an ideal resistor, has current and voltage in phase. Reactance exchanges energy with electric or magnetic fields and creates a phase shift. For a real component, impedance combines resistive and reactive effects. The magnitude of a component’s opposition is not enough to know whether current leads or lags; the sign of the reactance matters.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Practical ESR and leakage mean real capacitors can dissipate power too. Do not treat ideal reactance formulas as complete component ratings.

worked.heading: Worked case · Reactance and resistance are not the same quantity
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: At f = 100 Hz a 10 µF capacitor has |X_C| ≈ 159 Ω.
Its impedance is approximately −j159 Ω.
A 159 Ω resistor has the same magnitude but dissipates real power; the capacitor ideally returns stored energy each cycle.
worked.conclusion: The capacitor introduces phase shift and stores/returns energy; the resistor ideally dissipates energy without reactive phase shift.

reflection.ask: What is the key distinction between an ideal capacitor and a same-magnitude resistor in AC?
reflection.answer: The capacitor introduces phase shift and stores/returns energy; the resistor ideally dissipates energy without reactive phase shift.

goldTeaching.sectionNote: Use paper/simulation or approved protected low-voltage training only. Scope ground clips, inductive transients, charged capacitors, mains transformers and motor circuits create real hazards.

pages.title: Recognize resonance before calculating it
pages.text: An inductor and capacitor can exchange energy at a particular natural frequency.
pages.remember: Inductive X_L and capacitive |X_C|.
pages.sourceLesson: From reactance to impedance, phase, and resonance

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

For an ideal LC pair, f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)). At this frequency the magnitudes of X_L and X_C are equal. In an ideal series RLC network they cancel algebraically, leaving impedance near the series resistance; in parallel arrangements behavior differs and depends on topology/loss. The peak sharpness is controlled by damping and the quality factor Q, not just by L and C.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Do not claim a large coil current is safe simply because impedance approaches R at resonance; resonance can cause large component voltages even at modest source voltage.

worked.heading: Worked case · Recognize resonance before calculating it
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: For L = 10 mH and C = 100 nF, f₀ ≈ 5.03 kHz.
At that frequency X_L ≈ 316 Ω and |X_C| ≈ 316 Ω, which cancel in ideal series combination.
worked.conclusion: Inductive X_L and capacitive |X_C|.

reflection.ask: Which two reactances match in magnitude at an ideal LC resonance?
reflection.answer: Inductive X_L and capacitive |X_C|.

pages.title: Select real reactive components from specifications
pages.text: The nominal capacitance or inductance is the beginning of a replacement decision, not the whole decision.
pages.remember: For example: rated voltage, polarity, ESR/ripple-current rating, temperature and service life.
pages.sourceLesson: Component families, ratings, magnetism, and machines

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

For a capacitor, evaluate effective C, voltage rating, polarity, ESR, ripple current, temperature, dielectric and lifetime. For an inductor, check L at actual current, saturation and temperature limits, DC winding resistance, core loss and self-resonant frequency. A part that fits and measures correctly on an LCR meter may still perform badly under its actual bias and switching conditions.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Do not swap electrolytic polarity or test unknown capacitor energy by manually shorting leads. Manufacturer guidance and qualified procedures control work.

worked.heading: Worked case · Select real reactive components from specifications
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A 22 µH inductor operates at 1 A in a converter.
Two catalog choices are both 22 µH, but one saturates at 0.7 A and the other at 3 A.
The first is unsuitable even though the nominal inductance matches.
worked.conclusion: For example: rated voltage, polarity, ESR/ripple-current rating, temperature and service life.

reflection.ask: Which three ratings matter beyond the µF value for an electrolytic capacitor?
reflection.answer: For example: rated voltage, polarity, ESR/ripple-current rating, temperature and service life.

pages.title: Magnetic fields lead to motors, relays and transformers
pages.text: The fields around coils create force and coupling: the same principle explains devices that seem very different.
pages.remember: No. The coil circuit and switched-contact circuit have independent voltage/current ratings.
pages.sourceLesson: Component families, ratings, magnetism, and machines

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

A current-carrying winding creates a magnetic field; adding a magnetic core can direct it and increase coupling. A relay uses the field to move contacts. A motor uses electromagnetic torque to move a rotor, while a transformer transfers AC energy between windings by a changing common flux. Those are distinct applications with distinct insulation, ratings and hazards. Current must be evaluated in the actual winding and contact/load circuit separately.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Never assume relay contacts provide safe isolation without checking insulation ratings, creepage/clearance and intended application.

worked.heading: Worked case · Magnetic fields lead to motors, relays and transformers
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A 12 V relay coil draws 50 mA.
Coil power is 0.60 W.
Its contacts may be rated to switch much higher voltage/current, but the contact rating says nothing about the coil voltage or how to suppress the inductive release transient.
worked.conclusion: No. The coil circuit and switched-contact circuit have independent voltage/current ratings.

reflection.ask: Does a relay contact rating of 5 A mean its coil requires 5 A?
reflection.answer: No. The coil circuit and switched-contact circuit have independent voltage/current ratings.

pages.title: Measure and explain a reactive fault
pages.text: A good technician compares the predicted time behavior with a controlled measurement and checks safety first.
pages.remember: Verify units and actual R and C values before replacing components or altering the test.
pages.sourceLesson: Component families, ratings, magnetism, and machines

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

On a protected low-voltage circuit, record the expected RC or RL time constant, stimulus amplitude, observation point and probe influence. If the observed exponential rise is ten times slower, first verify the R/C/L unit conversions and actual measured component values. In electrolytic capacitors, ESR and leakage can cause symptoms not captured by the ideal time constant. The test result is evidence; the fault diagnosis remains a hypothesis until alternatives are ruled out.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Simulated tests demonstrate reasoning; only supervised physical measurement establishes practical equipment-handling evidence.

worked.heading: Worked case · Measure and explain a reactive fault
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: An RC step nominally has R = 2 kΩ and C = 10 µF, so τ = 20 ms.
A measured τ near 200 ms suggests a tenfold discrepancy: wrong decade resistor, 100 µF instead of 10 µF, or an unexpected circuit path.
worked.conclusion: Verify units and actual R and C values before replacing components or altering the test.

reflection.ask: What is the first useful check for a tenfold time-constant error?
reflection.answer: Verify units and actual R and C values before replacing components or altering the test.

examples.title: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

detail.problem: A 10 kΩ resistor charges a 10 µF capacitor from a 5 V step. Find τ and approximate voltage after one τ.
steps: After one τ, the capacitor has completed about 63% of the change.
After about 5τ = 0.5 s, it is near the final value.
detail.answer: τ = 0.1 s; Vc at one τ is about 3.15 V.
detail.transfer: A scope cursor can test both the predicted time and voltage on the charging curve.

examples.title: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

detail.problem: A 10 kOhm resistor charges a 100 uF capacitor from 0 V toward 5 V. Find tau and estimate voltage after one tau and five tau.
steps: After one tau, Vc≈0.632 x 5 V = 3.16 V.
After five tau, the capacitor is above 99% of the way to 5 V, roughly 4.97 V.
The current is initially 5/10k=0.5 mA and decreases as Vc rises.
detail.answer: tau=1 s; about 3.16 V at 1 s and approximately 5 V by 5 s.
detail.meaning: The time constant predicts the shape and timing of a real charging waveform.

examples.title: Component families, ratings, magnetism, and machines

detail.problem: A 5 V relay coil measures 125 Ω. Estimate steady current and coil power.
steps: Check whether the proposed driver can safely sink 40 mA plus margin.
Verify the datasheet coil rating; measured resistance is only a first estimate.
detail.answer: About 40 mA and 0.20 W.
detail.transfer: A microcontroller pin often cannot drive that coil directly, motivating a transistor and flyback diode.

examples.title: Component families, ratings, magnetism, and machines

detail.problem: A transformer has 500 primary turns and 100 secondary turns. The primary receives 120 Vrms. Estimate secondary voltage and ideal secondary current if the primary current is 50 mA.
steps: Turns ratio Np/Ns=500/100=5.
Ideal power in≈120*0.05=6 W.
Ideal Is≈6/24=0.25 A; real current will be limited by losses and ratings.
detail.answer: About 24 Vrms and 0.25 A idealized secondary current at 6 W.

pages.title: From resistance to frequency-dependent opposition
pages.text: An AC network can be understood by extending the DC concept of opposition with stored energy and timing.
pages.remember: An inductor; X_L doubles while |X_C| halves.
pages.sourceLesson: From reactance to impedance, phase, and resonance

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

Resistance R converts electric energy to heat; reactive components store and return some of it each cycle. Capacitive reactance |X_C| = 1/(2πfC) becomes smaller as frequency rises, while inductive reactance X_L = 2πfL increases. In an AC problem, identify the signal frequency first, convert µF/mH into base units, and check that the chosen model is sinusoidal steady state. The calculated ohms are not a DC resistance reading.
Limits and the technician’s decision
A real capacitor/coil also has loss resistance and parasitics. The ideal relationship may fail near self-resonance and at extreme temperatures or currents.

worked.heading: Worked case · From resistance to frequency-dependent opposition
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: At 2 kHz a 1 µF capacitor has |X_C| ≈ 79.6 Ω; a 10 mH coil has X_L ≈ 125.7 Ω.
At 4 kHz the first falls to 39.8 Ω and the second rises to 251.3 Ω.
worked.conclusion: An inductor; X_L doubles while |X_C| halves.

reflection.ask: At twice the frequency, which part offers larger ideal reactance: a capacitor or an inductor?
reflection.answer: An inductor; X_L doubles while |X_C| halves.

goldTeaching.sectionNote: Use paper/simulation or approved protected low-voltage training only. Scope ground clips, inductive transients, charged capacitors, mains transformers and motor circuits create real hazards.

pages.title: Impedance is a magnitude with phase
pages.text: A single AC impedance includes how much a signal is opposed and how current is shifted relative to voltage.
pages.remember: The resistive and reactive contributions are perpendicular phasor components.
pages.sourceLesson: From reactance to impedance, phase, and resonance

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

In phasor form, Z = R + jX, where X = X_L − |X_C| for a series RLC circuit. j denotes a 90-degree rotation between resistive and reactive components. The magnitude is |Z| = √(R² + X²) and phase φ = arctan(X/R) with the appropriate quadrant. A positive X means inductive behavior and lagging current; negative X means capacitive behavior and leading current. This is why you cannot simply add magnitudes of reactances to calculate current.
Limits and the technician’s decision
The sign of phase depends on the declared current and voltage reference convention. State that convention explicitly in reports.

worked.heading: Worked case · Impedance is a magnitude with phase
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A series circuit has R = 30 Ω and net X = +40 Ω.
Then |Z| = 50 Ω and φ ≈ +53.1°.
At 10 Vrms source, Irms = 10/50 = 0.2 A, with current lagging source voltage.
worked.conclusion: The resistive and reactive contributions are perpendicular phasor components.

reflection.ask: Why is √(30²+40²) correct instead of 30+40 for impedance magnitude?
reflection.answer: The resistive and reactive contributions are perpendicular phasor components.

pages.title: Series RLC response changes with frequency
pages.text: In a series network the same current flows through R, L and C, but their voltages have different phase relationships.
pages.remember: Current lags voltage in the usual passive sign convention.
pages.sourceLesson: From reactance to impedance, phase, and resonance

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

Compute X_L and X_C at the signal frequency, subtract to find net X, then calculate |Z|. At low frequency a capacitor often dominates; at high frequency an inductor does. At ideal series resonance, their reactances cancel and current is limited by R and real losses. The component voltages can still be much larger than the source voltage due to reactive energy exchange.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Do not add RMS component voltages as ordinary scalars; use phasor relationships. Always check reactive component voltage and current ratings.

worked.heading: Worked case · Series RLC response changes with frequency
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: On a 10 Vrms source, current ≈ 70.7 mA, lagging.
worked.conclusion: Current lags voltage in the usual passive sign convention.

reflection.ask: A circuit is inductive when X_L is greater than |X_C|. Does current lead or lag the source voltage?
reflection.answer: Current lags voltage in the usual passive sign convention.

pages.title: Resonance is cancellation, not zero impedance everywhere
pages.text: The phrase “at resonance” means something specific to circuit topology and losses.
pages.remember: Series resistance and other real losses; net reactive opposition cancels.
pages.sourceLesson: From reactance to impedance, phase, and resonance

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

For the ideal LC relationship, f₀ = 1/(2π√LC). In an ideal series RLC circuit at f₀, X_L = |X_C| and Z = R, so series current peaks. For a parallel RLC network, source input impedance may peak instead as branch reactive currents cancel; details depend on the arrangement and nonideal losses. Resonance is a family of behaviors, not a claim that all circuits short or open.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Series reactive component voltages may exceed applied source voltage; this example is analytical, not permission to energize an unverified resonant circuit.

worked.heading: Worked case · Resonance is cancellation, not zero impedance everywhere
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: In series, R = 50 Ω and 5 Vrms imply current ≈ 0.10 A at ideal resonance.
worked.conclusion: Series resistance and other real losses; net reactive opposition cancels.

reflection.ask: At ideal series resonance, what limits the current?
reflection.answer: Series resistance and other real losses; net reactive opposition cancels.

pages.title: Voltage/current phase diagrams are physical evidence
pages.text: The phase angle tells you where energy is stored and returned within each AC cycle.
pages.remember: 45° lag.
pages.sourceLesson: From reactance to impedance, phase, and resonance

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

A pure resistor’s voltage and current are in phase. A pure inductor has voltage leading current by 90°; a pure capacitor has current leading voltage by 90°. For a mixed series RLC, current phase depends on the net reactance sign. An oscilloscope can compare two safe, appropriately referenced signals to estimate phase from time shift Δt over period T: φ = 360° × Δt/T, with sign determined by which trace leads.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Two channels on a common-ground bench scope may not safely measure across arbitrary floating components. A paper/isolated model is the default.

worked.heading: Worked case · Voltage/current phase diagrams are physical evidence
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A 1 kHz pair of sine waves has period 1 ms.
Trace B peaks 0.25 ms after Trace A.
worked.conclusion: 45° lag.

reflection.ask: If a sine trace lags another by one-eighth of a period, what phase difference is that?
reflection.answer: 45° lag.

pages.title: Filters use impedance to choose what passes
pages.text: A frequency-selective network allocates more or less of an input signal to its output depending on frequency.
pages.remember: The chosen output node changes which component’s frequency-dependent voltage is measured.
pages.sourceLesson: From reactance to impedance, phase, and resonance

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

An RC low-pass with output at C is approximated by |H| = 1/√(1+(f/fc)²) and fc = 1/(2πRC) with negligible load. A high-pass output across R reverses the qualitative behavior. An LC network can shape a band-pass or notch response. Start with topology and where the output is taken; a capacitor by itself does not define filter type. Measure input and output under the same defined load.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Source impedance and load can move the actual cutoff; filter names are qualitative until a specified transfer curve is measured.

worked.heading: Worked case · Filters use impedance to choose what passes
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: For R = 1 kΩ and C = 10 nF, fc ≈ 15.9 kHz.
Below cutoff, unloaded low-pass magnitude is near 1; at cutoff it is about 0.707; well above cutoff it trends downward.
worked.conclusion: The chosen output node changes which component’s frequency-dependent voltage is measured.

reflection.ask: Why can the same RC components form different filter types?
reflection.answer: The chosen output node changes which component’s frequency-dependent voltage is measured.

pages.title: Decibels, cutoff and bandwidth
pages.text: A measured filter needs explicit criteria for what counts as passed or suppressed.
pages.remember: About 0.50, not 0.707.
pages.sourceLesson: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

Voltage transfer gain in dB is 20 log10(|Vout/Vin|) for a defined transfer ratio. For first-order filters the familiar −3 dB magnitude point corresponds to an amplitude ratio of roughly 0.707 relative to passband. Bandwidth is a specified frequency span, often between cutoff frequencies, not simply the highest frequency displayed. Q ≈ f₀/BW for a resonant system under the applicable definition; higher Q corresponds to a narrower fractional bandwidth.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Do not confuse −3 dB in voltage with half the amplitude; it corresponds to approximately half the power under matched conditions.

worked.heading: Worked case · Decibels, cutoff and bandwidth
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A band-pass peaks at 10 kHz and has specified −3 dB edges of 9.5 and 10.5 kHz.
BW = 1.0 kHz and Q ≈ 10 kHz/1 kHz = 10.
worked.conclusion: About 0.50, not 0.707.

reflection.ask: What is the approximate amplitude ratio at −6 dB?
reflection.answer: About 0.50, not 0.707.

pages.title: From impedance to an equivalent circuit
pages.text: Complex network behavior becomes manageable when you replace carefully identified parts with their correct frequency-specific impedances.
pages.sourceLesson: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

For a resistor, Z_R = R; an inductor, Z_L = jωL; a capacitor, Z_C = 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC), with ω = 2πf. Series impedances add as complex numbers; parallel branches combine by reciprocals as in DC circuit analysis. Calculate in rectangular form, then convert to magnitude/phase for expected current or output response. This keeps the signs and conservation laws visible.
Limits and the technician’s decision
A DC ohmmeter or a single LCR reading cannot establish the full transfer behavior across multiple frequencies.

worked.heading: Worked case · From impedance to an equivalent circuit
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A 100 Ω resistor in series with a 10 mH inductor at 1 kHz gives Z = 100 + j62.8 Ω.
Its magnitude is ≈118.1 Ω, not 162.8 Ω.
Phase is +32.1°.

reflection.ask: What is Z for a 100 nF capacitor at 1 kHz in ideal phasor notation?

pages.title: Sinusoidal versus pulsed inputs: interpret with care
pages.text: A frequency-response transfer formula applies directly to sinusoidal steady state; pulses contain many frequencies.
pages.remember: It removes or attenuates the higher frequency components needed for sharp transitions.
pages.sourceLesson: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

A symmetric square wave has a fundamental plus higher odd harmonics. A low-pass that attenuates those harmonics produces rounded transitions. If a circuit rings after a step, it may contain underdamped LC dynamics. The waveform’s rise time, overshoot, ringing frequency and final level help separate capacitive loading, inductive resonance and source limitations.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Never claim that one waveform alone identifies the failed component; verify loading, instrument compensation and alternate explanations.

worked.heading: Worked case · Sinusoidal versus pulsed inputs: interpret with care
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A 1 kHz square wave through a filter with 2 kHz cutoff retains its fundamental but attenuates faster edge harmonics; the output corners round even though the repetition rate stays at 1 kHz.
worked.conclusion: It removes or attenuates the higher frequency components needed for sharp transitions.

reflection.ask: Why does a low-pass alter the shape of a square wave?
reflection.answer: It removes or attenuates the higher frequency components needed for sharp transitions.

pages.title: Reading a response curve
pages.text: A graph is only useful when its axes, reference level, test stimulus and load are stated.
pages.remember: A factor of 10 in voltage amplitude under the stated transfer definition.
pages.sourceLesson: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

On a magnitude-versus-frequency plot, mark passband behavior, −3 dB crossings or other specified cutoff, slope and any resonance peaks. A log-frequency axis increases by multiplicative decades; a plot dropping 20 dB per decade shows a factor-of-ten amplitude reduction each decade. Check whether the ratio is voltage, power or a calibrated instrument reference. Add phase response when a timing or stability judgment depends on it.
Limits and the technician’s decision
A mislabeled “dB” axis without reference can make a technically correct plot impossible to interpret.

worked.heading: Worked case · Reading a response curve
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A low-pass shows 0 dB at 100 Hz, −3 dB at 1 kHz, and −23 dB near 10 kHz.
The decade above cutoff drops about 20 dB; that is compatible with a first-order roll-off in its asymptotic region.
worked.conclusion: A factor of 10 in voltage amplitude under the stated transfer definition.

reflection.ask: A +20 dB voltage transfer is what amplitude ratio?
reflection.answer: A factor of 10 in voltage amplitude under the stated transfer definition.

pages.title: Loading changes the network under test
pages.text: An instrument becomes part of the circuit when you connect it; the nominal schematic is no longer the whole system.
pages.remember: It becomes 0.5 MΩ effective resistance due to the parallel connection.
pages.sourceLesson: Characterize a filter or resonant network like a technician

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

A generator has finite source impedance; a scope and probe have input resistance and capacitance. A 10× passive probe often loads less than a 1× probe, but always consult the actual probe specifications. Across a large-value resistor, a modest probe input can change the divider ratio. This changes the measured cutoff, gain and even apparent resonant Q.
Limits and the technician’s decision
A surprising measurement is not immediate proof the circuit is wrong; include the instrument as part of the model.

worked.heading: Worked case · Loading changes the network under test
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A divider uses 1 MΩ upper and 1 MΩ lower resistance for an ideal half-supply output.
A 1 MΩ input meter placed in parallel with the lower 1 MΩ makes it 0.5 MΩ, and the measured ratio becomes 0.5/(1+0.5) = 1/3 rather than 1/2.
worked.conclusion: It becomes 0.5 MΩ effective resistance due to the parallel connection.

reflection.ask: What happens to the bottom leg of a 1 MΩ divider when a 1 MΩ instrument is placed across it?
reflection.answer: It becomes 0.5 MΩ effective resistance due to the parallel connection.

pages.title: A decade error has a recognizable signature
pages.text: Many apparent filter faults are mistakes in component identification, units or source loading.
pages.remember: The cutoff falls by a factor of 10.
pages.sourceLesson: Characterize a filter or resonant network like a technician

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

Because fc = 1/(2πRC), making C ten times larger reduces fc by ten. Changing L or C in f₀ = 1/(2π√LC) shifts resonance by a square-root factor, not one-for-one. A 10× probe misconfiguration scales voltage reports but not necessarily time-axis frequency readings. Use the mathematical relationship to predict the direction and size of the error before changing a part.
Limits and the technician’s decision
A single magnitude sample cannot isolate a component fault. Verify topology, source, load, instrument setup and more sweep points.

worked.heading: Worked case · A decade error has a recognizable signature
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A design expects RC cutoff at 2 kHz; actual response is near 200 Hz.
A 10× larger C or 10× larger R is a plausible first hypothesis.
A resonant peak moving to 0.632× original suggests L or C increased by roughly 2.5×.
worked.conclusion: The cutoff falls by a factor of 10.

reflection.ask: If R increases 10× with C fixed, what happens to an RC low-pass cutoff?
reflection.answer: The cutoff falls by a factor of 10.

pages.title: Plan a repeatable RLC characterization
pages.text: The last step of analysis is to make an experiment that could show you are wrong.
pages.remember: At minimum: circuit and node schematic, calibrated or stated stimulus/scale/load, and defined measurements/frequency points.
pages.sourceLesson: Characterize a filter or resonant network like a technician

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

Document the predicted resonance or cutoff, safe stimulus, input/output nodes, load, generator settings, probe factor, measurement bandwidth, reference, frequency points and acceptance criterion. Sweep sufficiently below, around and above the predicted feature. Record amplitude and phase separately. Compare the shape of discrepancy with likely modeling or setup errors rather than changing several variables at once.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Use simulation or appropriately supervised isolated low-voltage training hardware; resonance can produce elevated local component stresses.

worked.heading: Worked case · Plan a repeatable RLC characterization
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A computed series resonance is 5 kHz.
Simulate points at 1, 3, 4.5, 5.0, 5.5, 7 and 15 kHz while holding input level.
If measured peak is broad rather than sharp, look for damping resistance and loading rather than declaring the resonance equation invalid.
worked.conclusion: At minimum: circuit and node schematic, calibrated or stated stimulus/scale/load, and defined measurements/frequency points.

reflection.ask: What three pieces of information make a filter-response test reproducible?
reflection.answer: At minimum: circuit and node schematic, calibrated or stated stimulus/scale/load, and defined measurements/frequency points.

pages.title: Complete a traceable RLC fault argument
pages.text: A meaningful conclusion follows the circuit model, the measured evidence and an alternative-explanation check.
pages.remember: Stated model/prediction, reproducible observations, and a discriminating next measurement with alternatives considered.
pages.sourceLesson: Characterize a filter or resonant network like a technician

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

Before naming a bad component, identify whether the frequency response has shifted, gained unexpected damping or changed its passband level. Use predicted f₀ or fc to estimate which component parameter would move the signature in the observed direction. Document the source and load conditions. If the data comes from a simulation, call it modeled evidence rather than a hands-on measurement. The result should communicate which measurement would most efficiently distinguish the remaining hypotheses.
Limits and the technician’s decision
A difference in oscillator/source settings or probe load can mimic a shift. Describe conditions before inferring device failure.

worked.heading: Worked case · Complete a traceable RLC fault argument
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: An RLC network predicted to resonate at 3 kHz is measured near 2.1 kHz.
The ratio is 0.70.
Because f₀ ∝ 1/√LC, an LC product roughly twice the expected value could explain it.
Check component markings and actual effective capacitance/inductance before changing any part.
worked.conclusion: Stated model/prediction, reproducible observations, and a discriminating next measurement with alternatives considered.

reflection.ask: What are the three parts of a defensible AC-network conclusion?
reflection.answer: Stated model/prediction, reproducible observations, and a discriminating next measurement with alternatives considered.

examples.title: From reactance to impedance, phase, and resonance

detail.problem: At 1 kHz, a series circuit has R = 100 Ω, XL = 200 Ω, and XC = 50 Ω. Find |Z| and current from 10 Vrms.
steps: Net X = XL − XC = 150 Ω inductive.
Magnitude check: current must be lower than 10/100 = 100 mA because added reactance increases |Z|.
detail.answer: About 180 Ω and 55.5 mA rms, with inductive phase.
detail.transfer: A scope can compare resistor voltage (current reference) with source voltage to observe the phase direction.

examples.title: From reactance to impedance, phase, and resonance

detail.problem: A series circuit has R=100 ohm, L=10 mH, and is driven at 1 kHz. Find Xl, impedance magnitude, phase angle, and current from a 5 Vrms source.
steps: Phase=atan(62.8/100)=about +32.1 degrees, so the circuit is inductive and current lags voltage.
detail.answer: Xl≈62.8 ohm, |Z|≈118 ohm, phase≈+32 degrees, current≈42 mA rms.
detail.meaning: Reactance changes both the amount of current and its phase relative to the source.

examples.title: Characterize a filter or resonant network like a technician

detail.problem: A low-pass response has the expected shape but cutoff is 10× lower than calculated.
steps: Because shape is correct, topology is probably correct.
A 10× frequency shift implies the RC or LC product is wrong by a predictable factor.
Recheck prefixes and actual marked/measured values before rewiring.
Include source/load impedance if component values are correct.
detail.answer: Prioritize value/prefix/effective-impedance checks.
detail.transfer: Pattern-based diagnosis reduces random edits in filters and sensor front ends.

examples.title: Characterize a filter or resonant network like a technician

detail.problem: A band-pass RLC network is expected to peak near 5 kHz, but the measured peak is near 3.5 kHz and much broader.
steps: A lower resonant frequency means the effective LC product is larger than expected.
A broader/lower peak means damping/loss is greater: higher series resistance, inductor winding loss, capacitor ESR, or loading can contribute.
Measure actual L/C if possible and inspect source/load resistance before changing components.
Repeat the sweep with the same stimulus and documented measurement points after one controlled change.
detail.answer: The data suggests both a resonance shift and increased damping; verify reactive values and losses/loading separately.
detail.meaning: A response curve contains more information than a pass/fail point and can separate value errors from loss.

examples.title: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

detail.problem: A 10 kΩ resistor charges a 10 µF capacitor from a 5 V step. Find τ and approximate voltage after one τ.
steps: After one τ, the capacitor has completed about 63% of the change.
After about 5τ = 0.5 s, it is near the final value.
detail.answer: τ = 0.1 s; Vc at one τ is about 3.15 V.
detail.transfer: A scope cursor can test both the predicted time and voltage on the charging curve.

guided.text: Calculate Xc for 0.1 uF at 100 Hz, 1 kHz, and 10 kHz. Describe the trend before calculating.
For R=220 ohm and Xc=220 ohm in series, find impedance magnitude and phase angle.
Choose L=10 mH and C=100 nF. Calculate resonant frequency and explain what happens to net reactance at that frequency.
For a predicted 2 kHz cutoff, choose a five-frequency characterization set and explain why each point is useful.
A function generator says 2 Vpp with a 50 ohm source setting. Explain why the actual open-circuit voltage may differ and how you would verify it.
Sketch how increased series resistance changes the height and width of a series-resonance current peak.

teachBack: Explain Xc, Xl, impedance, phase, and resonance as one connected story. Use a series RLC example to show why resonance is not 'zero voltage' and how real resistance affects the response.

Explain how you would characterize an unknown low-pass or resonant network from scratch. Include source/load assumptions, frequency selection, amplitude/phase evidence, and how you would distinguish wrong component value from excessive loss.

Explain why capacitor voltage and inductor current cannot change instantaneously in the ideal model. Use one RC time-constant example and one inductive flyback example to connect the equations to observed waveforms.

questions.prompt: For an ideal capacitor driven by a sinusoidal voltage, how does its current relate to voltage?
choices: The capacitor permits only DC current.
questions.explanation: Capacitor current is proportional to the rate of change of its voltage. An ideal inductor has the opposite phase relation.

questions.prompt: A first-order RC low-pass filter is used to smooth a signal. Which components of the input are attenuated more strongly?
choices: Every frequency by exactly the same ratio
questions.explanation: A low-pass passes lower frequencies more readily and increasingly attenuates higher ones.

questions.prompt: Two tuned circuits have the same resonant frequency. Which has the higher Q?
choices: The one with the narrower bandwidth
The one with the wider bandwidth
Both must have the same Q
The one with no frequency selectivity
questions.explanation: For the usual resonator definition, Q = resonant frequency divided by bandwidth.

questions.prompt: A series impedance is 3 + j4 Ω. What are its magnitude and type?
questions.explanation: Magnitude is √(3² + 4²) = 5 Ω. Positive imaginary reactance indicates inductive behavior under the usual convention.

questions.prompt: Frequency doubles while L stays fixed. What happens to ideal inductive reactance?
questions.explanation: Correct. XL = 2πfL, so it changes directly with frequency.

questions.prompt: A series circuit has R=30 Ω and X=+40 Ω. What is |Z|?
At twice the frequency, ideal inductive reactance is:
questions.explanation: XL=2πfL.

questions.prompt: Series RLC: L=25 mH and C=100 nF. Resonance is approximately:
In an ideal series RLC with XL greater than XC, current usually:
questions.explanation: Net reactance is inductive, so current lags in standard convention.

questions.prompt: An unloaded first-order RC low-pass has magnitude at fc of approximately:
questions.explanation: At the −3 dB cutoff amplitude ratio is 1/√2.

questions.prompt: A resonance has f0=10 kHz and −3 dB bandwidth 1 kHz. Q is approximately:
questions.explanation: Q≈f0/BW=10 for the applicable resonator definition.

questions.prompt: Z=100+j62.8 Ω has magnitude closest to:
The measured RC filter cutoff is a decade lower than expected; likely first check?
choices: Any tenfold R or C value/prefix discrepancy
questions.explanation: fc inversely scales with RC, so a tenfold shift suggests value/units/loading checks.

pages.title: Current creates magnetic field
pages.text: Magnetic effects are not limited to permanent magnets; every electric current creates a surrounding magnetic field.
pages.remember: Not by itself; flux through the coil must change with time.
pages.sourceLesson: Component families, ratings, magnetism, and machines

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

A straight wire produces a field whose direction follows a right-hand rule for conventional current. A coil brings individual turns’ fields together; the core and air gap influence flux. Magnetic flux is measured in webers, and changing flux can induce an electromotive force (Faraday’s law). Lenz’s law gives the direction of the induced effect: it opposes the change that produced it, consistent with energy conservation.
Limits and the technician’s decision
A right-hand rule is a directional model, not a permission to work on energized high-current windings. Use the schematic reference direction consistently.

worked.heading: Worked case · Current creates magnetic field
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: Move a magnet toward a coil and the induced voltage has one polarity; reverse the motion and polarity reverses.
The induced voltage depends on speed and geometry, not simply the presence of a stationary magnet.
worked.conclusion: Not by itself; flux through the coil must change with time.

reflection.ask: Will a stationary magnetic field induce a sustained voltage in a motionless, fixed coil?
reflection.answer: Not by itself; flux through the coil must change with time.

pages.title: Transformer action begins with changing flux
pages.text: A transformer transfers energy between magnetically coupled windings using time-varying magnetic flux.
pages.remember: The induced secondary voltage depends on the rate of flux change; constant flux produces no sustained secondary emf.
pages.sourceLesson: Component families, ratings, magnetism, and machines

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

Alternating voltage on the primary creates changing core flux, which induces voltage in secondary turns. For an ideal transformer Vp/Vs = Np/Ns and Ip/Is ≈ Ns/Np; real devices have copper loss, core loss and leakage. A constant steady DC voltage does not sustain ordinary transformer action and may saturate a suitable AC-designed core. A winding is not automatically isolated just because two wires look separate; the construction defines isolation and insulation ratings.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Never connect an unknown transformer directly to wall power. Mains transformers and stored energy require qualified supervision; numeric examples are paper cases.

worked.heading: Worked case · Transformer action begins with changing flux
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A 120-turn primary and 60-turn secondary have ideal voltage ratio 2:1.
If the primary sees a small, safe AC test signal of 6 Vrms, expected secondary is about 3 Vrms before loading and losses.
worked.conclusion: The induced secondary voltage depends on the rate of flux change; constant flux produces no sustained secondary emf.

reflection.ask: Why does a conventional transformer require changing magnetic flux?
reflection.answer: The induced secondary voltage depends on the rate of flux change; constant flux produces no sustained secondary emf.

pages.title: Motor and generator: opposite energy directions
pages.text: Motors and generators share electromagnetic principles but use energy in opposite directions.
pages.remember: Generator: mechanical to electrical; motor: electrical to mechanical.
pages.sourceLesson: Component families, ratings, magnetism, and machines

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

Current-carrying conductors experience force in magnetic fields, producing torque in a motor. A moving conductor or changing flux can induce a voltage, allowing a generator to deliver electric energy when mechanical work is supplied. Back electromotive force in a spinning motor reduces its effective applied voltage and alters current. At stall, back EMF is low and current can be much higher than during normal rotation; controller and winding ratings matter.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Mechanical motion, rotating parts, high currents and stored energy pose real risks. This lesson uses models and manufacturer-specified safe trainer setups only.

worked.heading: Worked case · Motor and generator: opposite energy directions
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A DC motor draws 0.2 A when spinning freely but 1.5 A briefly at startup.
That does not necessarily mean a short: reduced speed means less opposing back EMF.
Sustained stall can overheat a winding.
worked.conclusion: Generator: mechanical to electrical; motor: electrical to mechanical.

reflection.ask: What is the energy conversion in a generator versus a motor?
reflection.answer: Generator: mechanical to electrical; motor: electrical to mechanical.

pages.title: Core materials, turns and magnetic loss
pages.text: Magnetic components work because material and geometry shape flux, but real cores impose limits.
pages.remember: At fixed voltage and turns it can increase flux excursion and approach saturation.
pages.sourceLesson: Component families, ratings, magnetism, and machines

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

More turns generally increase induced voltage at a given flux rate, while suitable magnetic cores improve coupling. Laminated cores can reduce eddy-current losses at mains frequencies, while ferrites often serve higher switching frequencies. Hysteresis and eddy currents dissipate energy as heat. Too much volt-seconds or DC bias can saturate a core, raising magnetizing current and causing overheating. These are why frequency and voltage ratings matter for transformers.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Core substitutions require electromagnetic and thermal specifications; same physical size does not establish interchangeability.

worked.heading: Worked case · Core materials, turns and magnetic loss
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A transformer designed for 60 Hz may saturate if driven at the same RMS voltage but much lower frequency, because flux swing roughly scales with applied voltage divided by frequency and turns.
worked.conclusion: At fixed voltage and turns it can increase flux excursion and approach saturation.

reflection.ask: Why can running an AC transformer at lower frequency cause trouble?
reflection.answer: At fixed voltage and turns it can increase flux excursion and approach saturation.

pages.title: Relay coils and contacts are different circuits
pages.text: A relay lets a relatively small control circuit actuate a separate switching path, but their ratings are independent.
pages.remember: No. Control-coil rating and switched-load/contact rating are separate.
pages.sourceLesson: Component families, ratings, magnetism, and machines

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

An electromechanical relay has a coil, armature and contacts. Normally open contacts close when operated; normally closed contacts open. Contact voltage/current, load type and switching life are independent from coil voltage/current. Contact bounce can produce multiple transitions. The coil is inductive, so a transistor driver typically needs properly selected suppression. A wiring diagram distinguishes control contacts from the load path.
Limits and the technician’s decision
Check relay contact rating for inductive versus resistive loads and certification for safe isolation. Do not experiment with wall power.

worked.heading: Worked case · Relay coils and contacts are different circuits
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A 12 V coil that draws 60 mA uses P = VI = 0.72 W.
Its contacts might be rated for 2 A at a specified DC voltage, but that contact rating neither tells you the coil drive current nor authorizes mains switching.
worked.conclusion: No. Control-coil rating and switched-load/contact rating are separate.

reflection.ask: Does a relay marked “10 A contacts” require 10 A through its coil?
reflection.answer: No. Control-coil rating and switched-load/contact rating are separate.

pages.title: Relay coil release transients and suppression
pages.text: When coil current is interrupted, stored magnetic energy must go somewhere.
pages.remember: It allows coil current to decay through a relatively low-voltage path instead of permitting a larger reverse voltage.
pages.sourceLesson: Read a datasheet and design a relay/inductive-load interface

paragraphs: Understand the physical model

Because v = L di/dt, a fast attempted current decrease can produce a high voltage across a coil and its driver. A properly oriented flyback diode across a DC relay coil provides a path for current as the coil decays; this commonly slows relay release. Other clamps (Zener, TVS, RC networks) may be appropriate depending on voltage, load and release-time requirements. The suppression component must match the coil, polarity, energy and switching arrangement.
Limits and the technician’s decision
A reversed or shorted clamp can create an unintended supply short. Do not apply a generic “always add a diode” rule to AC coils or time-critical relays.

worked.heading: Worked case · Relay coil release transients and suppression
worked.scenario: Predict each result before reading the calculation and compare it with the underlying physical model.
steps: A driver switches off 100 mA in a 50 mH coil.
Stored energy is ½ × 0.05 × 0.1² = 0.00025 J.
The clamp arrangement controls how that energy dissipates and how quickly current falls.
worked.conclusion: It allows coil current to decay through a relatively low-voltage path instead of permitting a larger reverse voltage.

reflection.ask: Why may a freewheel diode increase a relay’s release time?
reflection.answer: It allows coil current to decay through a relatively low-voltage path instead of permitting a larger reverse voltage.
