sections.teachingSpecification: Define prerequisites; teach concept physically and quantitatively; demonstrate a reasoned worked example with labeled visual and units when applicable.

sections.title: Impedance, shielding, termination and bonding
sections.teachingSpecification: Define prerequisites; teach concept physically and quantitatively; demonstrate a reasoned worked example with labeled visual and units when applicable.

sections.title: Testing, crimping, splicing and connectors
sections.teachingSpecification: Define prerequisites; teach concept physically and quantitatively; demonstrate a reasoned worked example with labeled visual and units when applicable.

objectives.title: List wire types and construction
List wire gauges used for various purposes
Explain construction of coaxial cable and the impedance characteristics
List common identifications for copper cables in standards, such as #18 and #24 diameter in the American Wire Gauge (AWG) and UTP cable in ANSI/TIA 568
Explain major differences between copper, coaxial and fiber optic cables
Describe impedance and its causes:
Explain reasons for maintaining a cable’s characteristics
Explain the effects of proper and improper termination
Explain the purposes and types of cabling grounding (bonding) and common conventions used in electrical / electronic work
Describe splicing knowledge and ability of coaxial and copper cable
Explain types of fiber splices
Briefly explain testing methods for all three types of cables and compare decibel (dB) loss measurements and techniques
Compare the fittings and connectors used in cabling and list potential defects a technician may encounter
Describe proper crimping of communications wiring connectors
Explain how cable prep tools are used and demonstrate proper and improper crimp applications

pages.title: Wire construction, gauge, and identification
pages.text: Wire and cable differ by conductor material, solid/stranded construction, insulation/jacket, shielding, twist and intended environment. Stranded wire tolerates flexing better; solid conductors hold shape and are common in fixed wiring/board work. American Wire Gauge is inverse: a smaller AWG number means a larger conductor diameter/cross-section and generally lower resistance/higher current capacity when installation conditions are comparable. Gauge selection also depends on insulation temperature, bundle/ambient conditions, length/voltage drop, connector limits and code/application requirements. Communications cable identification includes pair/category and pinout conventions; UTP uses twisted pairs to improve balanced-noise rejection, while shielded cable adds a conductive screen that must be terminated/bonded according to the system design. Never infer allowable current from gauge alone without the governing application.
pages.sourceLesson: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

pages.title: Coax, copper pairs, fiber, impedance, and termination
pages.text: Coaxial cable uses a center conductor, dielectric, surrounding shield and outer jacket. That geometry plus dielectric determines characteristic impedance, commonly 50 Ω for many RF systems and 75 Ω for many video/CATV systems. Characteristic impedance is not the same as the DC resistance measured end-to-end. Twisted copper pair carries balanced signals whose performance depends on pair geometry/twist and controlled termination. Fiber carries light rather than electrical current and is immune to ordinary electromagnetic pickup but has optical-loss, bend and connector-cleanliness constraints. At high frequencies, mismatched impedance or poor termination creates reflections, ringing and standing waves even when a DC continuity test passes. Maintaining cable geometry, connector type and specified termination is therefore part of preserving signal integrity.
pages.sourceLesson: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

pages.title: Use end-to-end and sectional tests to isolate cable faults
pages.text: Start with connector identity/pinout and visual inspection. Continuity/short testing can separate open conductors, crossed pins, and shorts on copper harnesses. Wiggle/strain testing may reproduce intermittent faults if performed safely and within procedure. Known-good substitution can separate cable from electronics when compatibility is controlled. For high-speed/optical faults, use the appropriate certification, TDR, power/loss, or other instrument rather than assuming a basic DMM can prove performance.
pages.sourceLesson: Terminate, inspect, continuity-test, and isolate a connection fault

pages.title: Bonding, splicing, crimping, and cable preparation
pages.text: Cable shields and bonds provide controlled reference, fault/noise paths and electromagnetic containment when applied according to the system design. A shield connection that is too long, corroded or landed at the wrong point can perform poorly at high frequency. Copper/coax splicing requires the correct connector or splice method, preserved conductor/shield geometry, strain relief and inspection. Fiber splices are commonly fusion splices (controlled arc joins prepared fiber ends) or mechanical splices (aligned ends held by a precision fixture/index-matching system); both require clean, properly cleaved fiber. Crimp quality depends on matching terminal, conductor gauge and crimp tool/die, stripping the correct length without nicking strands, placing conductor/insulation correctly, completing the full tool cycle and performing visual/pull/electrical checks. The wrong die or over/under-strip can create intermittent faults that continuity may miss under motion.
pages.sourceLesson: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

pages.title: Cable testing, dB loss, connectors, and defects
pages.text: Cable tests must match the property being verified. Continuity/resistance tests find opens, shorts and gross connection problems in copper/coax but do not prove bandwidth, impedance or crosstalk. TDR-type methods locate impedance discontinuities by reflection. Fiber power meters/light sources measure insertion loss; OTDR methods can locate events and distance-dependent loss. Decibels express ratios: for power, dB = 10 log10(P2/P1); a negative insertion-loss result means less delivered power. Connector defects include bent/recessed pins, poor shield contact, contamination, incorrect keying, damaged latch/strain relief, excessive untwist, end-face contamination/scratches and wrong connector/cable impedance. A technician records source/reference level, test configuration and acceptance limit so a dB number can be reproduced.
pages.sourceLesson: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

pages.title: Connectors and terminations are part of signal integrity
pages.text: A connector must match pinout, current/voltage, impedance where relevant, retention, environment, and signal type. Poor crimp, shield termination, wrong coax impedance, excessive untwist, fiber contamination, or a damaged ferrule can create intermittent or frequency-dependent faults. Ground/bonding and shield strategy follow the system design; a shield connected poorly at high frequency can have enough inductance to lose effectiveness. Test methods must match the medium: DMM continuity for simple copper paths, TDR/cable certification for higher-speed copper/coax, optical power/loss or OTDR for fiber when appropriate.
pages.sourceLesson: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

pages.title: Choose media from signal, environment, and termination
pages.text: Conductors have resistance, capacitance, inductance, shielding, impedance, bandwidth, and mechanical limits. Coax controls geometry/impedance and shielding; twisted pair improves rejection of common interference; ribbon/harness wiring emphasizes organized point-to-point connection. Connector family is not enough—keying, pinout, gender, impedance, rating, strain relief, and termination quality matter.
pages.remember: Signal type + impedance/bandwidth + environment + connector/pinout + workmanship.
pages.sourceLesson: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

pages.title: Termination quality is a process, not a beep
pages.text: A copper crimp requires the correct wire gauge/type, terminal, strip length, conductor position, insulation support, tool and die, and complete crimp cycle. Inspect conductor and insulation crimp geometry, perform the required pull or mechanical check, then verify continuity and absence of shorts. For coax, preserve center conductor, dielectric, shield geometry, connector preparation, and impedance. For fiber, cleanliness, cleave/splice quality, bend radius, connector endface, and optical-loss evidence matter. Each medium has its own acceptance evidence.
pages.sourceLesson: Terminate, inspect, continuity-test, and isolate a connection fault

pages.title: Mechanical workmanship is electrical reliability
pages.text: Strip length, conductor damage, crimp height/engagement, insulation support, strain relief, bend radius, keying, and label clarity affect resistance and intermittency. Follow the connector/tool manufacturer’s process and objective workmanship criteria. A continuity beep alone can miss high resistance, wrong pin mapping, intermittent strain, or shielding faults.
pages.remember: Inspect, map, continuity/resistance-test, strain-test safely, then signal-test if required.
pages.sourceLesson: Terminate, inspect, continuity-test, and isolate a connection fault

pages.title: Audio and video systems are source–processing–path–load chains
pages.text: Audio stages may include transducer, preamplifier, filtering, power amplifier, cable, and speaker. Video adds timing/bandwidth and format conversion. A fault at one boundary affects everything downstream. Hum/noise, attenuation, clipping, loss of one channel, and sync/display symptoms suggest different locations. Match impedance/level conventions and avoid assuming connector shape defines the signal.
pages.remember: Trace direction and expected level at each block boundary.
pages.sourceLesson: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

pages.title: Optical links move modulated light through a controlled path
pages.text: A source launches light into fiber; connectors/splices/bends add loss/reflection; a receiver converts light to electrical signal. Multimode and single-mode differ in core size, sources, reach, and handling. Attenuation budgets use dB. Never look into a fiber or source; invisible radiation can injure eyes. Fiber shards are a skin/eye hazard and require controlled disposal.
pages.remember: Treat every fiber as active until verified with the approved method; never inspect by eye.
pages.sourceLesson: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

pages.title: Document orientation and reference
pages.text: Harness errors are often created by viewing a connector from the wrong side. Record mating-face versus wire-side view, pin numbering, keying, colors, shield/drain, and revision. Photograph or draw the connector orientation with a clear reference. A correct continuity table with the wrong orientation label can still cause the next technician to miswire the system. Traceability is part of workmanship.
pages.sourceLesson: Terminate, inspect, continuity-test, and isolate a connection fault

pages.title: Interfacing, distortion, conflicts, fault isolation, and signal levels
pages.text: Interfacing alarm/security, entertainment and information products requires compatible signal type, level, reference, impedance and connector/protocol. Audio levels are relative categories rather than one exact voltage: microphone level is small, line level is larger but intended for high-impedance line inputs, headphone outputs can drive moderate loads, and speaker outputs deliver far greater current/power to low-impedance loads. Connecting a speaker-level output to a microphone input can clip or damage the input. Distortion can come from clipping/overload, crossover/nonlinearity, bad source material, speaker excursion/thermal limit, grounding/hum, bandwidth limitation or sampling/codec artifacts. To isolate a glitch between discrete units, substitute a known-good source/load/cable or observe the signal at the interface while changing one element. Ground loops may create hum; incompatible formats or levels may create silence, clipping, noise or intermittent behavior.
pages.sourceLesson: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

pages.title: Transmission media change the physical path, not the information goal
pages.text: Copper pairs, coaxial cable, PCB traces, and optical fiber carry signals using different physical mechanisms and have different impedance, shielding, bandwidth, loss, connector, and handling concerns. Twisted pair uses geometry and differential signaling/noise rejection in many applications; coax provides a controlled unbalanced shielded path; fiber carries modulated light and is immune to electrical ground loops but introduces optical power/connector cleanliness/bend/splice concerns. Continuity alone cannot prove high-frequency performance or optical loss.
pages.sourceLesson: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

examples.title: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

detail.problem: An optical link has +0 dBm launch power, 8 dB path loss, and receiver sensitivity −10 dBm.
steps: Received power = 0 dBm − 8 dB = −8 dBm.
Margin relative to −10 dBm sensitivity is 2 dB.
Positive margin predicts possible operation, but 2 dB may be poor allowance for aging/temperature/contamination.
Check specified design margin and connector cleanliness/measurement uncertainty.
detail.answer: Predicted −8 dBm with 2 dB margin.
detail.transfer: dB path budgets use addition/subtraction even though underlying power ratios multiply.

examples.title: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

detail.problem: A 50 ohm RF source is connected through a 75 ohm coax segment and adapters to a 50 ohm load. The system shows reflections.
steps: The physical connection may have continuity, but characteristic-impedance mismatches exist at 50-to-75 and 75-to-50 ohm transitions.
At sufficiently high frequency/fast edge, part of the wave reflects at each discontinuity.
A DMM continuity test cannot characterize this reflection behavior.
Use the correct impedance cable/connectors or characterize with appropriate RF/TDR methods; compare with a known matched load.
detail.answer: The fault is signal-integrity mismatch, not simple DC continuity.
detail.meaning: Media and connector selection must match the signal's frequency/impedance requirements.

examples.title: Terminate, inspect, continuity-test, and isolate a connection fault

detail.problem: A harness passes continuity on the bench but fails when moved.
steps: Reproduce while monitoring the affected conductor and reference.
Inspect strain relief, partial crimp, conductor nick, connector latch, and pin retention.
Avoid aggressive flexing that can worsen damage or create unsafe exposure.
Correct the confirmed mechanical/electrical cause and repeat static plus controlled-movement tests.
detail.answer: Treat it as an intermittent connection requiring mechanical and electrical evidence.
detail.transfer: Intermittent harness faults are common and can masquerade as firmware resets or sensor errors.

examples.title: Terminate, inspect, continuity-test, and isolate a connection fault

detail.problem: A 6-pin harness intermittently loses a sensor signal when the cable is bent near one connector. Static continuity usually passes.
steps: Record the exact bend/strain condition that reproduces the fault.
Inspect crimp strain relief, conductor entry, pin retention, and any sharp bend near the connector.
Monitor continuity/resistance while gently reproducing the allowed movement, or use signal capture if the fault occurs only in operation.
If one conductor opens under strain, reterminate with the correct terminal/tool and verify pull/continuity plus the original movement condition.
detail.answer: Treat it as an intermittent termination/conductor fault and reproduce it under controlled strain before retermination and retest.
detail.meaning: Static pass/fail measurements can miss mechanically induced intermittent faults.

examples.title: Retention: workmanship, cabling, measurement, and safety

detail.problem: After header rework, continuity is correct but the board intermittently resets when the cable moves.
steps: Static continuity does not rule out weak joint, pin retention, strain, or supply dip.
Inspect under magnification and monitor relevant rail/reset while applying only safe controlled movement.
Separate harness, connector, and board joint by substitution or boundary measurement.
Repair confirmed cause; repeat static, movement, and functional tests.
detail.answer: Use mechanical plus time-domain electrical evidence; do not accept continuity alone.
detail.transfer: The case becomes a strong portfolio story when documented honestly from symptom to retest.

questions.prompt: Within the usual American Wire Gauge system, how does 18 AWG compare with 24 AWG?

18 AWG has a smaller conductor diameter.

questions.prompt: Which check is appropriate for a newly crimped low-voltage harness?

questions.prompt: What is the safe rule for an unknown fiber?

Explain what R-C-L substitution equipment is and its purposes

pages.title: An oscilloscope is a voltage-versus-time instrument
pages.text: Vertical scale sets volts per division; horizontal scale sets seconds per division. Probe attenuation must match the channel setting or displayed amplitude is wrong by a factor such as ten. Trigger level and slope choose a repeatable point in the waveform so it appears stable. DC coupling preserves offset; AC coupling blocks the DC component for viewing small variation. Period is horizontal divisions × time/div, and frequency is 1/period.
pages.remember: Before measuring, state expected amplitude, offset, frequency, and reference location.
pages.sourceLesson: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

pages.title: Oscilloscope controls and spectrum analyzer operation
pages.text: An oscilloscope displays voltage versus time. Vertical scale controls volts/division; vertical position establishes where the trace sits; coupling selects DC, AC or ground/reference behavior; probe factor must match the probe; horizontal time/division controls the visible time span; trigger source/level/slope/event stabilizes acquisition relative to a repeatable point; bandwidth/sample-rate/acquisition settings affect what can be trusted. Measure amplitude only after confirming probe factor and reference, and distinguish peak, peak-to-peak and RMS. A spectrum analyzer displays amplitude/power versus frequency. Center frequency and span choose the region, reference level and input attenuation protect/scale the input, and resolution bandwidth (RBW) trades frequency resolution against sweep/noise behavior; video bandwidth (VBW) smooths displayed noise. A spectrum analyzer answers “what frequencies are present,” while a scope answers “how does voltage change with time.” Neither input should be exposed to an unknown signal beyond its rated level.
pages.sourceLesson: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

pages.title: Signal generators, frequency counters, RCL substitution, and ESR meters
pages.text: A signal generator supplies a controlled test stimulus such as sine, square, pulse, sweep, audio/RF or function-generator output. Set waveform, amplitude, offset, frequency, source impedance and load assumptions before connection. A frequency counter measures event rate by counting cycles over a gate/timebase or related technique; accuracy is limited by timebase quality, gate time, trigger/signal level, noise and bandwidth. R-C-L substitution boxes provide known selectable resistance, capacitance or inductance so a technician can test whether circuit behavior changes when a suspected value is replaced under safe conditions; they are not a substitute for understanding voltage/current/power ratings. ESR meters estimate equivalent series resistance, particularly useful for finding degraded electrolytic capacitors whose capacitance may look plausible while internal loss is high. In-circuit readings can be influenced by parallel paths, so the measurement method and circuit state matter.
pages.sourceLesson: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

pages.title: Analog/digital meters, construction, safety, loading, and leads
pages.text: An analog meter movement responds to current and uses resistors/shunts/rectification to create ranges; a digital multimeter converts an input through protection/ranging and an ADC to a numeric display. Voltage mode presents high input impedance and is connected in parallel. Current mode routes current through a low-value shunt/fuse and is inserted in series; placing a current-configured meter across a source can create a dangerous short. Resistance/continuity applies an internal test source and belongs on a de-energized circuit. Meter loading occurs because the instrument is not infinite impedance: a low input resistance can pull a high-impedance node away from its normal voltage. Safety means correct category/voltage/current rating, intact case/leads/fuses, correct jack and mode, and staying within the task’s permitted energy level. Test leads are equipment: inspect insulation, finger guards, shrouds and tips, and replace damaged leads rather than taping over unsafe damage.
pages.sourceLesson: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

pages.title: Logic probes and logic pulsers: observe versus stimulate
pages.text: A logic probe is an observing instrument for digital nodes. Referenced to circuit ground and operated within its supported logic-family/voltage range, it indicates logic HIGH, LOW, and on many probes pulsing/activity. It does not tell you that a HIGH is “good” unless the expected logic state and threshold family are known. A logic pulser is the complementary stimulus tool: it injects a brief controlled logic transition or pulse at a node so the technician can see whether downstream logic responds. Used with a logic probe, oscilloscope or logic analyzer, it can separate “the upstream stage never changes” from “the downstream stage cannot respond.” Before pulsing, verify circuit supply/logic family, node direction, drive capability and that forcing the node will not create destructive bus contention or violate an analog/sensitive node. Example: if an AND-gate output is stuck, verify its supply and static inputs, safely pulse one eligible input while the other is at the enabling state, and observe the output. If the input changes but the output never follows, the gate/output path becomes a stronger suspect.
pages.sourceLesson: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

pages.title: Dummy loads, rheostats, isolation transformers, Variacs, and potentiometers
pages.text: A dummy load substitutes a known electrical load so equipment can be tested without the real antenna, speaker or system; it must match impedance and dissipate expected power. A rheostat is a two-terminal use of a variable resistor to adjust current/resistance and must be rated for the resulting power. A potentiometer is a three-terminal variable divider; the wiper samples a fraction of the voltage between the ends, subject to loading. An isolation transformer provides galvanic isolation between primary and secondary so the secondary is not directly bonded to the source conductor in the same way; it does not make contact with both secondary conductors safe and does not remove stored/high-energy hazards. A Variac (variable autotransformer) adjusts AC voltage with a movable tap but normally provides no galvanic isolation. Therefore “Variac = isolation” is false. Transformer/Variac size matters because VA/current/insulation ratings must exceed the test load and fault demands.
pages.sourceLesson: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

pages.title: Meters are circuits connected to circuits
pages.text: A DMM does not observe without interaction. In voltage mode it presents a high input resistance so only a small current is drawn; in current mode it presents a very low-resistance shunt so branch current can be measured; in resistance mode it applies an internal test source. Those three modes require different physical connections. The wrong mode can create a fault: a current-configured meter placed across a supply effectively connects a low-resistance path across the source. Analog meters use a sensitive movement with resistor/shunt networks, while digital meters use protection, ranging, conversion, and a display. Understanding the internal idea explains loading and safety rather than reducing the meter to a knob position.
pages.sourceLesson: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

pages.title: Instrument choice follows the question
pages.text: A DMM is excellent for stable DC quantities and many low-frequency checks; a scope reveals time-varying amplitude, timing, ringing, glitches, and transients; a frequency counter can measure periodic frequency precisely under suitable signal conditions; a signal generator creates a known stimulus; a spectrum analyzer shows magnitude versus frequency; ESR and substitution tools answer component-specific troubleshooting questions. The correct instrument is the one that can observe the behavior that would distinguish your hypotheses without violating circuit or instrument limits.
pages.sourceLesson: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

pages.title: Read from rails and references into functional blocks
pages.text: Identify all sources, grounds/reference domains, protection, regulators, connectors, inputs, processing/amplification, outputs, and feedback. Mark test points at block boundaries. Nets with the same label are connected even when no line is drawn; crossing lines may not join unless marked. Power symbols can hide connections across pages, so build a rail inventory.
pages.remember: A signal has meaning only relative to its reference and operating condition.
pages.sourceLesson: Read diagram types and turn symbols into behavior

pages.title: A datasheet is conditional evidence
pages.text: Confirm part/package/revision, then pinout, absolute maximums, recommended conditions, electrical characteristics, timing, typical application, and layout notes. Values apply under stated temperature, voltage, load, and test circuits. Build an expected-value table with minimum/typical/maximum where available; do not promote a typical graph to a guaranteed specification.
pages.remember: Copy the condition with the number or the number loses its meaning.
pages.sourceLesson: Read diagram types and turn symbols into behavior

pages.title: Block diagrams, test points, signal tracing, and schematic fault location
pages.text: Troubleshooting begins by turning the product into functional stages: source/power, input conditioning, processing, drivers and output are common examples. A block diagram helps choose boundaries; the schematic provides component-level paths. Test points are deliberately accessible nodes chosen because their expected voltage, waveform, logic state or signal can prove whether a stage is operating. Signal tracing applies a known input, predicts what should appear at successive points, and finds the first boundary where expected behavior disappears or changes incorrectly. Tracing can proceed input-to-output, output-to-input or by half-split depending on access and risk. The goal is not to measure every point; it is to choose a point whose possible outcomes separate hypotheses. Always preserve common reference/ground and loading limits. Once the first bad boundary is located, the schematic narrows the suspect components/connections between the last-good and first-bad nodes.
pages.sourceLesson: Read diagram types and turn symbols into behavior

pages.title: Building wiring awareness and flowcharts
pages.text: Electronics technicians often interface equipment with building power, grounding, branch circuits, receptacles, low-voltage pathways and communications cabling. They need enough premises-wiring awareness to recognize source voltage, grounding/bonding context, breaker/branch identity, receptacle condition, separation requirements and when work belongs to a qualified electrician. This course does not authorize mains installation or energized premises work. Flowcharts are different from schematics: they represent decisions, sequence and process state using start/end, action and decision branches. A flowchart can describe a troubleshooting procedure, boot sequence or test algorithm even when no electrical connection is shown. Use a schematic to understand where current/signal can travel and a flowchart to understand what action or decision happens next.
pages.sourceLesson: Read diagram types and turn symbols into behavior

pages.title: Antennas, feedlines, impedance matching, SWR/VSWR, and feedline types
pages.text: An antenna converts guided RF energy on a feedline into radiated electromagnetic energy and performs the reciprocal receive function. Feedline types include coaxial cable (unbalanced, shielded, common at 50 Ω or 75 Ω), balanced twin-lead/ladder line (two spaced conductors with characteristic impedance set by geometry/dielectric), waveguide (a hollow/structured guide used especially at microwave frequencies above cutoff), and PCB transmission lines such as microstrip/stripline between RF circuitry and connectors/antennas. Feedlines have characteristic impedance determined by geometry/material, not ordinary DC resistance. When load/antenna impedance does not match the feedline/source, part of the wave reflects. Standing-wave ratio expresses mismatch; VSWR = (1+|Γ|)/(1-|Γ|), with 1:1 ideal. Causes include wrong cable/connector impedance, antenna detuning, damaged/wet cable, poor termination and frequency change. A dummy load matched to the system lets a technician separate transmitter/feedline/antenna problems without radiating through the antenna.
pages.sourceLesson: RF, modulation, antennas, transmission, and telecom blocks

pages.title: Spectrum bands and radio tuning/alignment
pages.text: Frequency bands group services and equipment by spectrum region—for example HF, VHF, UHF and microwave ranges, with exact allocations controlled by regulators and service rules. A technician should recognize the names/order and use current allocation tables rather than memorize every service edge indefinitely. Tuning means adjusting or electronically selecting a resonant/synthesized path so the desired signal/channel is passed or generated. Older circuits may use variable capacitors/inductors and IF alignment; modern radios commonly use PLL synthesizers, digitally controlled filters and software calibration. Alignment is not random “tweaking”: establish the correct test signal, instrument/reference, order of adjustments and target from service documentation. Misalignment can reduce sensitivity, selectivity, power or spectral compliance.
pages.sourceLesson: RF, modulation, antennas, transmission, and telecom blocks

detail.problem: A waveform spans 4 vertical divisions at 0.5 V/div and one cycle spans 5 horizontal divisions at 200 µs/div.

detail.transfer: If the 10× probe is set to 10× but the channel assumes 1×, the amplitude display will be wrong even though the trace looks stable.

detail.problem: A 3.3 V digital output appears as 0.33 V on the oscilloscope, while a DMM reads 3.29 V.
steps: The DMM suggests the node's DC level is near 3.3 V.
A factor-of-ten scope discrepancy strongly suggests probe attenuation mismatch: for example a 10x probe with the channel set to 1x, or vice versa.
Verify probe switch position and channel probe factor before changing the circuit.
Also verify the ground/reference point and DC coupling.
detail.answer: Check probe attenuation/configuration and reference before concluding the digital output is only 0.33 V.
detail.meaning: Instrument configuration is part of the measurement and can create a false fault symptom.

detail.problem: A 100 MHz signal travels in free space. Estimate wavelength.
steps: Use λ = c/f.
λ ≈ 3 m.
In a cable, multiply by its velocity factor, so physical wavelength is shorter.
detail.answer: Approximately 3 m in free space.
detail.transfer: A quarter wavelength is about 0.75 m in free space before velocity/environment effects.

detail.problem: Find free-space wavelength at 2.4 GHz and estimate quarter wavelength.
steps: Quarter wavelength=0.03125 m=3.125 cm.
Real antennas/feedlines are affected by dielectric, geometry, end effects, and environment.
The calculation gives useful physical scale but is not a complete antenna design.
detail.answer: About 12.5 cm wavelength and 3.1 cm quarter wavelength in free space.
detail.meaning: Frequency sets the physical scale at which interconnect and antenna geometry become important.

questions.explanation: A spectrum analyzer shows frequency content. An oscilloscope typically shows amplitude versus time.

questions.prompt: Why use a suitably rated RF dummy load during a transmitter test?
choices: Absorb RF output into a known load while limiting unintended radiation

pages.title: Audio and video systems are source–processing–path–load chains
pages.text: Audio stages may include transducer, preamplifier, filtering, power amplifier, cable, and speaker. Video adds timing/bandwidth and format conversion. A fault at one boundary affects everything downstream. Hum/noise, attenuation, clipping, loss of one channel, and sync/display symptoms suggest different locations. Match impedance/level conventions and avoid assuming connector shape defines the signal.
pages.remember: Trace direction and expected level at each block boundary.
pages.sourceLesson: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

pages.title: Audio/video blocks, microphones, speakers, recording and playback
pages.text: A typical audio/video chain has source/transducer, conditioning/preamp, conversion or processing, transport/storage, power/driver stage and output/display/transducer. A dynamic microphone generates voltage from coil/magnet motion and usually needs no polarization power; a condenser microphone uses a capacitive element and active electronics and commonly requires bias/phantom power depending on type. A loudspeaker converts electrical current in a voice coil and magnetic field into motion; impedance, power, enclosure and thermal/mechanical limits matter. Recording converts the source signal into a stored representation—analog magnetic/physical or, commonly, sampled/quantized digital data through an ADC/codec. Playback reverses the path through decoding/DAC/amplification to the transducer. The technician follows signal level and format at each boundary rather than treating “audio” or “video” as one homogeneous signal.
pages.sourceLesson: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

pages.title: Interfacing, distortion, conflicts, fault isolation, and signal levels
pages.text: Interfacing alarm/security, entertainment and information products requires compatible signal type, level, reference, impedance and connector/protocol. Audio levels are relative categories rather than one exact voltage: microphone level is small, line level is larger but intended for high-impedance line inputs, headphone outputs can drive moderate loads, and speaker outputs deliver far greater current/power to low-impedance loads. Connecting a speaker-level output to a microphone input can clip or damage the input. Distortion can come from clipping/overload, crossover/nonlinearity, bad source material, speaker excursion/thermal limit, grounding/hum, bandwidth limitation or sampling/codec artifacts. To isolate a glitch between discrete units, substitute a known-good source/load/cable or observe the signal at the interface while changing one element. Ground loops may create hum; incompatible formats or levels may create silence, clipping, noise or intermittent behavior.
pages.sourceLesson: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

pages.title: Distortion, loading, buffering, and measurement error
pages.text: Distortion means the output is not a scaled/time-shifted version of the intended input. Clipping occurs when output swing reaches a limit; crossover distortion can appear near zero in poorly biased push-pull stages; slew-rate limiting distorts fast/large signals; overload, thermal/current limiting and nonlinear bias can add harmonics or compression. Measurement equipment can create apparent distortion or gain error by loading the circuit. A DMM or scope input has finite resistance and capacitance; a 1× scope probe often loads a high-impedance/high-frequency node more than a 10× probe. Reduce loading by selecting a higher-impedance probe/meter, using a 10× probe when appropriate, buffering the node, measuring at a lower-impedance test point, shortening grounds/leads, and accounting for bandwidth. A clean-looking waveform is not proof of the circuit’s unloaded behavior unless the instrument’s effect is considered.
pages.sourceLesson: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

pages.title: Amplifiers use supply energy to reproduce a signal with gain
pages.text: An amplifier does not create energy from the input signal. The input controls how supply power is delivered to the output. Voltage gain is Av=Vout/Vin under stated conditions; current and power gain are distinct quantities. Preamplifiers usually raise small signals before later processing, while line or driver stages interface between blocks or loads. Class A, B, AB, and switching amplifier classes differ in conduction and efficiency/distortion tradeoffs. Frequency response describes how gain and phase change with frequency, so a quoted 'gain of 10' is incomplete without frequency, load, supply, and output-quality conditions.
pages.sourceLesson: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

pages.title: Coax, copper pairs, fiber, impedance, and termination
pages.text: Coaxial cable uses a center conductor, dielectric, surrounding shield and outer jacket. That geometry plus dielectric determines characteristic impedance, commonly 50 Ω for many RF systems and 75 Ω for many video/CATV systems. Characteristic impedance is not the same as the DC resistance measured end-to-end. Twisted copper pair carries balanced signals whose performance depends on pair geometry/twist and controlled termination. Fiber carries light rather than electrical current and is immune to ordinary electromagnetic pickup but has optical-loss, bend and connector-cleanliness constraints. At high frequencies, mismatched impedance or poor termination creates reflections, ringing and standing waves even when a DC continuity test passes. Maintaining cable geometry, connector type and specified termination is therefore part of preserving signal integrity.
pages.sourceLesson: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

pages.title: Display technologies: LED, seven-segment, LCD, OLED, and tradeoffs
pages.text: Electronic displays convert electrical drive into controlled visible output. An LED emits light when forward-biased; current must be limited and polarity observed. A seven-segment display groups LEDs into segments that form numerals. Common-anode packages share positive supply and light a segment by pulling its cathode low; common-cathode packages share return and light a segment by driving its anode high. Multiplexed displays rapidly select digits to reduce wiring/driver count. An LCD is not normally self-emissive: an electric field changes liquid-crystal optical behavior, with a backlight often providing illumination; DC bias must be controlled according to the driver because sustained DC can damage/age segments. OLED pixels are emissive organic devices, providing high contrast and no backlight but with current/aging/burn-in considerations. Display choice balances brightness, power, contrast, viewing angle, lifetime, drive complexity, cost and environment.
pages.sourceLesson: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

pages.title: Optical and display devices convert between energy forms
pages.text: LEDs emit light when forward biased with controlled current; seven-segment displays arrange LEDs into numeric segments; LCDs modulate light and typically require a backlight for transmissive displays; OLED pixels emit their own light. Photovoltaic cells generate electrical output from illumination, photodiodes produce light-dependent current, phototransistors provide gain, and LDRs change resistance. Opto-isolators transfer a signal across a galvanic isolation barrier using an emitter/detector pair. These devices have polarity, current, speed, sensitivity, isolation, aging, and spectral constraints that matter in real circuits.
pages.sourceLesson: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

pages.title: Modulation, communications receivers, and radio usage
pages.text: Modulation changes a carrier or symbol stream to represent information. AM changes carrier amplitude; FM changes instantaneous frequency. Digital radio systems use symbol modulation/coding such as PSK/QAM families and multiple-access/network methods. CDMA is a code-division access technique, while GSM, LTE and 5G are generations/standards that combine modulation, coding and multiple-access methods—do not treat all four as interchangeable “modulations.” Communications radios are designed for two-way or service-specific transmit/receive operation, while commercial broadcast receivers are primarily one-way receivers. A generic receiver path is antenna/preselector → low-noise/RF amplifier → mixer/local oscillator (or direct-sampling equivalent) → IF/baseband filtering/amplification → demodulation/decoding → audio/data output. Automatic gain/control and synthesizers may support the chain. Troubleshooting follows signal level/frequency through these stages.

examples.title: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

detail.problem: An optical link has +0 dBm launch power, 8 dB path loss, and receiver sensitivity −10 dBm.
steps: Received power = 0 dBm − 8 dB = −8 dBm.
Margin relative to −10 dBm sensitivity is 2 dB.
Positive margin predicts possible operation, but 2 dB may be poor allowance for aging/temperature/contamination.
Check specified design margin and connector cleanliness/measurement uncertainty.
detail.answer: Predicted −8 dBm with 2 dB margin.
detail.transfer: dB path budgets use addition/subtraction even though underlying power ratios multiply.

examples.title: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

detail.problem: A 50 ohm RF source is connected through a 75 ohm coax segment and adapters to a 50 ohm load. The system shows reflections.
steps: The physical connection may have continuity, but characteristic-impedance mismatches exist at 50-to-75 and 75-to-50 ohm transitions.
At sufficiently high frequency/fast edge, part of the wave reflects at each discontinuity.
A DMM continuity test cannot characterize this reflection behavior.
Use the correct impedance cable/connectors or characterize with appropriate RF/TDR methods; compare with a known matched load.
detail.answer: The fault is signal-integrity mismatch, not simple DC continuity.
detail.meaning: Media and connector selection must match the signal's frequency/impedance requirements.

examples.title: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

detail.problem: An inverting op-amp uses Rin = 10 kΩ, Rf = 47 kΩ, and Vin = 0.20 V. Find ideal output.
steps: Check whether the supply rails and input common-mode permit this result.
Check load and bandwidth before expecting the ideal value physically.
detail.answer: Ideal Vout = −0.94 V.
detail.transfer: If powered from a single 0–5 V supply with no bias, a negative output request will clip near the lower rail.

examples.title: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

detail.problem: A non-inverting op-amp uses Rg=10 kOhm and Rf=40 kOhm with Vin=0.4 V. Supply is 0-5 V and the op-amp can swing only to about 0.2-4.8 V.
steps: Ideal gain=1+40k/10k=5.
Ideal output=0.4*5=2.0 V, inside the stated output range.
If Vin rises to 1.2 V, ideal output would be 6 V, impossible on a 5 V supply.
The real output saturates near its upper swing limit; the virtual-input-equality assumption no longer supports the linear gain equation.
detail.answer: 2.0 V is plausible for 0.4 V input; 6 V is not, so a 1.2 V input would drive the stage into saturation.
detail.meaning: Closed-loop formulas must be checked against supply and operating limits.

examples.title: RF, modulation, antennas, transmission, and telecom blocks

detail.problem: A 100 MHz signal travels in free space. Estimate wavelength.
steps: Use λ = c/f.
λ ≈ 3 m.
In a cable, multiply by its velocity factor, so physical wavelength is shorter.
detail.answer: Approximately 3 m in free space.
detail.transfer: A quarter wavelength is about 0.75 m in free space before velocity/environment effects.

questions.prompt: A microphone performs which conversion?
choices: Sound pressure variations into an electrical signal
An electrical signal into a visual image
DC power into radio frequency by definition
A stored file directly into mechanical cable strain

questions.prompt: A clean audio input becomes visibly clipped at the amplifier output. Which cause should be checked?

questions.prompt: An audio chain has a source, cable and amplifier. Which test helps isolate a suspect cable?

Raise every control to maximum first.
Assume continuity proves all high-frequency behavior.

questions.prompt: Why should a speaker-level output not be assumed safe for a microphone input?

A microphone input always accepts any power.
Audio frequency alone guarantees voltage compatibility.

pages.title: Photovoltaic cells, photodiodes, phototransistors, LDRs, materials, and symbols
pages.text: Photoelectronic devices convert light and electrical behavior in different ways. A photovoltaic cell generates voltage/current when photons create charge carriers in a semiconductor junction; greater illumination generally increases available photocurrent, while voltage/current depend on cell and load. Photodiodes produce light-dependent current and are often operated reverse-biased for speed/linearity or in photovoltaic mode for sensing. Phototransistors use light-generated base action to provide current gain and greater sensitivity with slower response. A photoresistor/LDR changes resistance with light level and is slower/nonlinear but simple for threshold controls. Common materials include silicon for many visible/near-IR devices and compound semiconductors such as GaAs/GaN families for other spectral/emission needs; exact spectral response comes from the datasheet. Schematic symbols distinguish resistor-with-light-arrows, diode-with-light-arrows and transistor-with-light-arrows. Light-activated controls convert sensor output into a threshold/analog/digital decision that then drives a relay, transistor, MCU input or other stage.
pages.sourceLesson: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

pages.title: Optical links move modulated light through a controlled path
pages.text: A source launches light into fiber; connectors/splices/bends add loss/reflection; a receiver converts light to electrical signal. Multimode and single-mode differ in core size, sources, reach, and handling. Attenuation budgets use dB. Never look into a fiber or source; invisible radiation can injure eyes. Fiber shards are a skin/eye hazard and require controlled disposal.
pages.remember: Treat every fiber as active until verified with the approved method; never inspect by eye.
pages.sourceLesson: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

pages.title: Cameras, opto-isolators, and broadband optical links
pages.text: Electronic cameras focus light onto an image sensor array (commonly CMOS), where pixels convert photons into charge/electrical signals that are read, amplified and converted to digital image data. Exposure depends on light, lens/aperture, integration time/shutter and sensor gain. An opto-isolator/opto-coupler contains a light emitter, usually an LED, and an isolated detector such as a phototransistor/photodiode. The light path transfers information while maintaining galvanic isolation between input and output circuits within the device ratings. Uses include isolating low-voltage control from higher-voltage power stages, breaking ground paths, isolated feedback and digital input/output. Isolation voltage, creepage/clearance, transfer ratio, speed and aging matter; an optocoupler is not an unlimited safety barrier. Broadband optical links encode/modulate information onto light through fiber; RF broadband links use electromagnetic carriers/antennas. Both have transmitter, medium/channel, receiver, bandwidth, attenuation/noise and link-budget concerns, but the physical medium and hazards differ.

pages.title: Audio/video blocks, microphones, speakers, recording and playback
pages.text: A typical audio/video chain has source/transducer, conditioning/preamp, conversion or processing, transport/storage, power/driver stage and output/display/transducer. A dynamic microphone generates voltage from coil/magnet motion and usually needs no polarization power; a condenser microphone uses a capacitive element and active electronics and commonly requires bias/phantom power depending on type. A loudspeaker converts electrical current in a voice coil and magnetic field into motion; impedance, power, enclosure and thermal/mechanical limits matter. Playback reverses the path through decoding/DAC/amplification to the transducer. The technician follows signal level and format at each boundary rather than treating “audio” or “video” as one homogeneous signal.
pages.sourceLesson: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

pages.title: Transmission media change the physical path, not the information goal
pages.text: Copper pairs, coaxial cable, PCB traces, and optical fiber carry signals using different physical mechanisms and have different impedance, shielding, bandwidth, loss, connector, and handling concerns. Twisted pair uses geometry and differential signaling/noise rejection in many applications; coax provides a controlled unbalanced shielded path; fiber carries modulated light and is immune to electrical ground loops but introduces optical power/connector cleanliness/bend/splice concerns. Continuity alone cannot prove high-frequency performance or optical loss.
pages.sourceLesson: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

pages.title: Connectors and terminations are part of signal integrity
pages.text: A connector must match pinout, current/voltage, impedance where relevant, retention, environment, and signal type. Poor crimp, shield termination, wrong coax impedance, excessive untwist, fiber contamination, or a damaged ferrule can create intermittent or frequency-dependent faults. Ground/bonding and shield strategy follow the system design; a shield connected poorly at high frequency can have enough inductance to lose effectiveness. Test methods must match the medium: DMM continuity for simple copper paths, TDR/cable certification for higher-speed copper/coax, optical power/loss or OTDR for fiber when appropriate.

examples.title: Junction behavior and semiconductor device roles

detail.problem: A 5 V supply drives a red LED approximated at 1.9 V with a 330 Ω resistor. Estimate current and resistor power.
steps: Resistor voltage = 5 − 1.9 = 3.1 V.
P resistor = I²R ≈ 0.029 W.
Verify the actual LED datasheet and current target; forward voltage is not exact.
detail.answer: About 9.4 mA and 29 mW in the resistor.
detail.transfer: This same load current becomes the minimum current the transistor switch must handle.

detail.problem: A low-side N-channel MOSFET switches a 12 V, 0.5 A load. The MOSFET has Rds(on)=0.08 ohm at the stated gate drive. Estimate conduction loss.
steps: This low conduction loss is only valid at the gate voltage for which Rds(on) is specified.
Switching losses, thermal environment, transients, and load type still require checking.
If the datasheet specifies Rds(on) only at 10 V gate drive, a 3.3 V MCU may not turn the device on fully.
detail.answer: About 20 mW conduction loss under the stated Rds(on) condition.
detail.meaning: A transistor part number is not enough; the control voltage and datasheet test condition determine the actual switching behavior.

State the assumed code range/reference and expected quantization.
Compare with an independent meter measurement if available.
detail.answer: Approximately 1.65 V.
detail.transfer: A correct formula with the wrong reference or alignment still yields a believable wrong result.

pages.title: RF systems move information through electromagnetic energy
pages.text: Frequency and wavelength are inversely related by lambda=v/f. At RF, conductor length and geometry become part of circuit behavior because signals propagate as waves rather than ideal instantaneous voltages. Antennas convert guided energy on a feedline to radiated fields and back. Polarization describes electric-field orientation. Reflection, diffraction, absorption, free-space loss, multipath, and environmental effects shape received signals. RF safety depends on frequency, power, antenna gain, duty cycle, distance, and exposure conditions; invisible energy is not automatically safe.
pages.sourceLesson: RF, modulation, antennas, transmission, and telecom blocks

pages.title: Antennas, feedlines, impedance matching, SWR/VSWR, and feedline types
pages.text: An antenna converts guided RF energy on a feedline into radiated electromagnetic energy and performs the reciprocal receive function. Feedline types include coaxial cable (unbalanced, shielded, common at 50 Ω or 75 Ω), balanced twin-lead/ladder line (two spaced conductors with characteristic impedance set by geometry/dielectric), waveguide (a hollow/structured guide used especially at microwave frequencies above cutoff), and PCB transmission lines such as microstrip/stripline between RF circuitry and connectors/antennas. Feedlines have characteristic impedance determined by geometry/material, not ordinary DC resistance. When load/antenna impedance does not match the feedline/source, part of the wave reflects. Standing-wave ratio expresses mismatch; VSWR = (1+|Γ|)/(1-|Γ|), with 1:1 ideal. Causes include wrong cable/connector impedance, antenna detuning, damaged/wet cable, poor termination and frequency change. A dummy load matched to the system lets a technician separate transmitter/feedline/antenna problems without radiating through the antenna.
pages.sourceLesson: RF, modulation, antennas, transmission, and telecom blocks

pages.title: Modulation places information on a carrier
pages.text: Amplitude, frequency, or phase can vary with information; digital schemes create related symbol patterns. A transmitter creates/amplifies/filter/signals to the antenna/path; a receiver selects, amplifies, converts/demodulates, and recovers information. Time-domain and frequency-domain views answer different questions. Harmonics, bandwidth, noise floor, and spurious signals appear in a spectrum.
pages.remember: Carrier/source → modulation → amplification/filter → path → selection/demodulation → output.
pages.sourceLesson: RF, modulation, antennas, transmission, and telecom blocks

pages.title: Modulation, communications receivers, and radio usage
pages.text: Modulation changes a carrier or symbol stream to represent information. AM changes carrier amplitude; FM changes instantaneous frequency. Digital radio systems use symbol modulation/coding such as PSK/QAM families and multiple-access/network methods. CDMA is a code-division access technique, while GSM, LTE and 5G are generations/standards that combine modulation, coding and multiple-access methods—do not treat all four as interchangeable “modulations.” Communications radios are designed for two-way or service-specific transmit/receive operation, while commercial broadcast receivers are primarily one-way receivers. A generic receiver path is antenna/preselector → low-noise/RF amplifier → mixer/local oscillator (or direct-sampling equivalent) → IF/baseband filtering/amplification → demodulation/decoding → audio/data output. Automatic gain/control and synthesizers may support the chain. Troubleshooting follows signal level/frequency through these stages.
pages.sourceLesson: RF, modulation, antennas, transmission, and telecom blocks

pages.title: Modulation and receivers transform representation
pages.text: AM varies carrier amplitude; FM varies instantaneous frequency; digital systems use symbol modulation/coding such as PSK/QAM families along with access/network methods. A receiver may include preselection/RF amplification, mixing/local oscillator or direct sampling, IF/baseband filtering, demodulation/decoding, and output. Spectrum displays magnitude/power versus frequency and reveal carrier, bandwidth, harmonics, noise, and spurs. Time-domain scope and frequency-domain spectrum views answer different questions.
pages.sourceLesson: RF, modulation, antennas, transmission, and telecom blocks

pages.title: Feedlines have characteristic impedance
pages.text: Coaxial cable, balanced twin-lead/ladder line, waveguide, and PCB microstrip/stripline are examples of transmission paths used at RF. Characteristic impedance is set by geometry and material properties, not ordinary DC resistance. A mismatch between source/feedline/load reflects part of the wave. Reflection coefficient and VSWR quantify mismatch; a 1:1 VSWR is ideal. Wrong cable impedance, damaged or wet cable, poor connectors, antenna detuning, or incorrect termination can create high reflected energy. A matched dummy load helps separate transmitter/feedline/antenna problems without relying on the antenna.
pages.sourceLesson: RF, modulation, antennas, transmission, and telecom blocks

pages.title: Reactance is frequency-dependent opposition
pages.text: Capacitive reactance is XC = 1/(2πfC), so it falls as frequency or capacitance rises. Inductive reactance is XL = 2πfL, so it rises as frequency or inductance rises. Both are measured in ohms, but unlike ideal resistance they exchange stored energy with the source and create phase relationships. At DC steady state an ideal capacitor appears open and an ideal inductor appears short, but their transients still matter.
pages.remember: Higher frequency: capacitor opposes less, inductor opposes more.
pages.sourceLesson: From reactance to impedance, phase, and resonance

pages.title: Reactance is frequency-dependent opposition
pages.text: In AC circuits, capacitors and inductors oppose changing signals in different ways. Capacitive reactance is Xc = 1/(2 pi f C), so a capacitor presents less opposition as frequency rises. Inductive reactance is Xl = 2 pi f L, so an inductor presents more opposition as frequency rises. Reactance is measured in ohms but is not ordinary resistance: ideal reactance stores and returns energy rather than dissipating average real power. That distinction produces phase shift. For an ideal capacitor, current leads voltage; for an ideal inductor, current lags voltage. Those phase relationships matter whenever resistance and reactance coexist.
pages.sourceLesson: From reactance to impedance, phase, and resonance

pages.title: RF behavior depends on frequency and physical geometry
pages.text: Wavelength λ = v/f; in free space v is approximately the speed of light, while cables have a velocity factor. Conductors and interconnects behave as transmission lines when length is significant relative to wavelength/rise time. Impedance mismatch produces reflection and standing-wave behavior. Antennas convert guided electrical energy to/from electromagnetic waves with pattern, polarization, bandwidth, and gain.
pages.remember: At high frequency, interconnect geometry becomes part of the circuit.
pages.sourceLesson: RF, modulation, antennas, transmission, and telecom blocks

pages.title: Impedance combines resistance and reactance as a vector
pages.text: In a simple series R–X circuit, magnitude |Z| = √(R² + X²), where net reactance is XL − XC. Current magnitude is V/|Z|. Resistance is the in-phase component; reactance is the quadrature component. Adding their magnitudes directly is generally wrong. The phase angle follows tan φ = X/R with sign showing inductive or capacitive behavior.
pages.remember: Draw the impedance triangle before reaching for the square root.
pages.sourceLesson: From reactance to impedance, phase, and resonance

pages.title: Resonance and transformation are controlled relationships
pages.text: At series resonance, XL and XC cancel, leaving minimum impedance in the ideal series RLC circuit and maximum current. The resonant frequency is f0 = 1/(2π√LC). A transformer uses magnetic coupling: Vp/Vs = Np/Ns ideally, while current ratio is inverse and power is approximately conserved except for losses. Transformers can change voltage/current levels and provide galvanic isolation, but they do not pass DC steady state.
pages.remember: State whether resonance is series or parallel and whether transformer values are ideal before interpreting the result.
pages.sourceLesson: From reactance to impedance, phase, and resonance

pages.title: Resonance is cancellation of opposite reactances
pages.text: At series resonance, Xl and Xc are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign, so their net reactance cancels and the series impedance is primarily resistive. The resonant frequency is f0 = 1/(2 pi sqrt(LC)). In a series RLC circuit, current is maximum near resonance because impedance magnitude is minimum. Q describes how sharply energy is exchanged relative to losses; bandwidth is related to resonance sharpness. Real circuits include source resistance, winding resistance, capacitor ESR, loading, and parasitics, so measured resonance can shift and broaden compared with the ideal calculation.
pages.sourceLesson: From reactance to impedance, phase, and resonance

pages.title: Wave propagation, fields, polarization, and wavelength
pages.text: Radio communication uses time-varying electromagnetic fields that propagate energy away from an antenna. The electric (E) and magnetic (H) fields are linked components of the propagating wave; electrostatic fields are associated with essentially static charge and do not by themselves describe a radiated RF wave. Polarization describes the orientation/time behavior of the wave’s electric field (for example horizontal, vertical or circular) and should match the receiving antenna for efficient coupling. In free space, wavelength and frequency satisfy λ = c/f, where c is approximately 3×10^8 m/s. Higher frequency therefore has shorter wavelength. Propagation is affected by free-space loss, reflection, diffraction, absorption, multipath and the environment. A technician uses frequency/wavelength to recognize antenna scale and cable/fixture behavior but follows approved RF-exposure boundaries rather than experimenting with transmit power.
pages.sourceLesson: RF, modulation, antennas, transmission, and telecom blocks

pages.title: A useful handoff separates observation, interpretation, and escalation
pages.text: Write: setup; expected result; observed trace/marker values; uncertainty/limitations; likely layer; safe next action. If the issue appears RF-specific beyond your competence or equipment, say what has been ruled out and escalate with evidence. For example, '3.3 V rail and SPI control remain within requirements; conducted spectrum shows new spur at X MHz after firmware build Y; antenna/radiated compliance not evaluated.' That statement is more useful than 'radio is bad.'
pages.sourceLesson: Measurement procedure, spectrum interpretation, and technical handoff

examples.title: Measurement procedure, spectrum interpretation, and technical handoff

detail.problem: A 50 MHz expected tone is absent, but the analyzer span is 1–10 MHz.
steps: The setup cannot display 50 MHz, so absence is not evidence of signal failure.
Set a safe center/span including 50 MHz and appropriate reference level.
Verify instrument/input path with a known source or documented check.
Only then compare expected tone, harmonics, and noise.
detail.answer: Correct the measurement window before troubleshooting the source.
detail.transfer: Instrument configuration belongs in the hypothesis tree.

examples.title: Measurement procedure, spectrum interpretation, and technical handoff

detail.problem: A 100 MHz signal shows an unexpected 200 MHz component 25 dB below the fundamental. You suspect second harmonic but the first capture used unknown RBW/attenuation.
steps: 200 MHz is exactly twice 100 MHz, so a second harmonic is plausible.
Because the original settings are incomplete, repeat under documented center/span, reference, attenuation, RBW/VBW, detector, and connection conditions.
Check whether the 200 MHz component tracks the 100 MHz source amplitude and whether it is present with a known-good source/path.
Report it as an observed harmonic candidate, not compliance failure, unless the proper standard/limit procedure is applied.
detail.answer: Reproduce with controlled settings, verify relationship to the source, and report the evidence with appropriate scope of claim.
detail.meaning: Spectrum interpretation is inseparable from instrument configuration and the requirement being evaluated.

examples.title: From reactance to impedance, phase, and resonance

detail.problem: At 1 kHz, a series circuit has R = 100 Ω, XL = 200 Ω, and XC = 50 Ω. Find |Z| and current from 10 Vrms.
steps: Net X = XL − XC = 150 Ω inductive.
Magnitude check: current must be lower than 10/100 = 100 mA because added reactance increases |Z|.
detail.answer: About 180 Ω and 55.5 mA rms, with inductive phase.
detail.transfer: A scope can compare resistor voltage (current reference) with source voltage to observe the phase direction.

questions.explanation: Wavelength equals propagation speed divided by frequency: 3 × 10⁸ / 10⁸ = 3 m.

choices: A significant impedance mismatch and reflected wave
The absence of any transmitted frequency
questions.explanation: Standing waves result from forward and reflected waves. A match minimizes reflection under the stated conditions.

questions.prompt: For a linearly polarized radio wave, polarization is defined by which orientation?
choices: The enclosure's longest edge in every case
The color of the feed cable
questions.explanation: Polarization concerns the electric field and affects coupling between transmit and receive antennas.

questions.prompt: Frequency doubles while L stays fixed. What happens to ideal inductive reactance?
questions.explanation: Correct. XL = 2πfL, so it changes directly with frequency.

pages.title: Telecom systems remain source–network–destination chains
pages.text: Telephone and data systems use signaling, switching/routing, transmission media, addressing/channelization, and endpoint conversion. Technician-level CETa work emphasizes terminology, block flow, measurements, connectors, and procedure. RF energy and transmitters require exposure controls; this course uses receive-only, low-energy simulation, prerecorded data, or compliant equipment—never unlicensed or unsafe transmitting.

pages.title: Two-way, cellular/wireless, and satellite communications
pages.text: Two-way radio systems include land-mobile, public-safety, maritime, aviation and other services, each with assigned channels, operating practices and regulatory requirements. A wireless telephone/data system connects a user device through a radio access network/base station to switching/routing/core networks and onward services. Modern cellular standards use cells, mobility management, channel/resource scheduling, authentication and packet data. Applicable standards depend on the system: ANSI/TIA-603 covers measurement/performance for certain land-mobile FM/PM equipment, the TIA-102 family covers Project 25 land-mobile digital radio, and cellular generations are primarily specified through 3GPP plus carrier/vendor requirements. The technician should identify the standard named for the actual product/service instead of assuming one document covers every wireless system. Satellite communication adds an uplink from earth to satellite, a transponder/payload that receives/translates/amplifies/routes, and a downlink to another earth terminal. Link performance depends on path loss, antenna gain, frequency, atmospheric effects, noise and alignment; satellite distance also creates noticeable propagation delay. Service category determines allowed frequency/power and installation practice.
pages.sourceLesson: RF, modulation, antennas, transmission, and telecom blocks

pages.title: Wired data/voice networks and POTS
pages.text: Wired data networks commonly use Ethernet over twisted pair/fiber: endpoints connect through switches at the local-link layer, while routers move IP packets between networks. Link indication does not prove IP, DNS or application success, and a continuity pass does not prove category/bandwidth performance. Traditional POTS (plain old telephone service) uses a two-wire tip/ring loop carrying DC loop current for off-hook signaling plus superimposed voice AC and higher-voltage ringing from the central-office/adapter side. Polarity conventions and exact voltages vary by system and country, so service documentation controls. Splices/terminations must preserve pair continuity and insulation and avoid shorts/grounds/crossed pairs. Troubleshooting separates physical pair fault, loop/ringing condition and network/service-side problem; do not treat telecom pairs as harmless simply because they are “low voltage,” because ringing/transients may be present.
pages.sourceLesson: RF, modulation, antennas, transmission, and telecom blocks

pages.title: Optical links move modulated light through a controlled path
pages.text: A source launches light into fiber; connectors/splices/bends add loss/reflection; a receiver converts light to electrical signal. Multimode and single-mode differ in core size, sources, reach, and handling. Attenuation budgets use dB. Never look into a fiber or source; invisible radiation can injure eyes. Fiber shards are a skin/eye hazard and require controlled disposal.
pages.remember: Treat every fiber as active until verified with the approved method; never inspect by eye.
pages.sourceLesson: Media, connectors, signal paths, and optical fundamentals

pages.title: Wire construction, gauge, and identification
pages.text: Wire and cable differ by conductor material, solid/stranded construction, insulation/jacket, shielding, twist and intended environment. Stranded wire tolerates flexing better; solid conductors hold shape and are common in fixed wiring/board work. American Wire Gauge is inverse: a smaller AWG number means a larger conductor diameter/cross-section and generally lower resistance/higher current capacity when installation conditions are comparable. Gauge selection also depends on insulation temperature, bundle/ambient conditions, length/voltage drop, connector limits and code/application requirements. Communications cable identification includes pair/category and pinout conventions; UTP uses twisted pairs to improve balanced-noise rejection, while shielded cable adds a conductive screen that must be terminated/bonded according to the system design. Never infer allowable current from gauge alone without the governing application.

pages.title: Telecom networks add infrastructure
pages.text: Two-way radio, cellular, satellite, Ethernet/data networks, and POTS use different physical/network architectures. Cellular devices depend on a radio-access network and core routing/authentication infrastructure. Satellite links include uplink, transponder/payload, and downlink with large path loss and delay. Wired Ethernet separates physical link from switching, IP routing, DNS, and application success. Traditional POTS uses a tip/ring loop with DC loop current plus voice/ringing behavior. Technician-level competence is recognizing the blocks, safe measurement boundaries, and documentation—not memorizing every allocation forever.

detail.problem: An optical link has +0 dBm launch power, 8 dB path loss, and receiver sensitivity −10 dBm.
steps: Received power = 0 dBm − 8 dB = −8 dBm.
Margin relative to −10 dBm sensitivity is 2 dB.
Positive margin predicts possible operation, but 2 dB may be poor allowance for aging/temperature/contamination.
Check specified design margin and connector cleanliness/measurement uncertainty.

detail.transfer: dB path budgets use addition/subtraction even though underlying power ratios multiply.

detail.problem: A 50 ohm RF source is connected through a 75 ohm coax segment and adapters to a 50 ohm load. The system shows reflections.
steps: The physical connection may have continuity, but characteristic-impedance mismatches exist at 50-to-75 and 75-to-50 ohm transitions.
At sufficiently high frequency/fast edge, part of the wave reflects at each discontinuity.
A DMM continuity test cannot characterize this reflection behavior.
Use the correct impedance cable/connectors or characterize with appropriate RF/TDR methods; compare with a known matched load.
detail.answer: The fault is signal-integrity mismatch, not simple DC continuity.
detail.meaning: Media and connector selection must match the signal's frequency/impedance requirements.

steps: 8N1 commonly has 1 start + 8 data + 1 stop = 10 bits.
Tchar ≈ 86.8 µs.
Maximum ideal character rate is about 11,520 per second before software/protocol overhead.
detail.answer: About 8.68 µs per bit and 86.8 µs per 8N1 character.
detail.transfer: A logic-analyzer cursor can verify baud by measuring bit width.

A 50 ohm system is connected to a badly mismatched antenna. Explain qualitatively what reflection and VSWR mean and how a dummy load helps isolate the fault.
Draw a generic superheterodyne-style receiver chain and identify where tuning, frequency conversion, filtering, and demodulation occur.
Compare twisted pair, coax, and fiber by signal mechanism, common application, major test method, and one handling concern.
Explain the difference between a common-anode and common-cathode seven-segment display and how segment drive polarity changes.
Compare photovoltaic cell, photodiode, phototransistor, and LDR by output behavior and a suitable application.

teachBack: Explain how frequency, wavelength, feedline impedance, antenna, modulation, and receiver blocks fit into one communication system. Include one mismatch/VSWR example and one reason spectrum and time-domain views are different.

Teach the differences among copper/coax/fiber media and among LED/LCD/OLED/photo devices. Then explain why continuity is only one kind of evidence and what instrument you would choose for a high-frequency or optical fault.
Explain an 8N1 UART frame from idle through stop bit, calculate bit time from baud, and describe how you would distinguish wrong baud from wrong voltage/wiring using raw waveform evidence.

questions.prompt: In traditional POTS terminology, what do tip and ring identify?
choices: The two conductors of a telephone pair
A microphone and a loudspeaker cone
questions.explanation: Tip and ring are conductor names in the telephone circuit, not a guarantee that a line is safe to touch.

questions.prompt: What does the downlink in a satellite communication system describe?
choices: Transmission from satellite toward a ground receiver
A cable connecting two resistors on a board
questions.explanation: Uplink and downlink distinguish direction relative to the satellite.

questions.prompt: Time-division multiplexing separates channels principally by what?
choices: Assigning each channel a separate building
Making every channel use the same data at once
Removing the need for timing synchronization
questions.explanation: TDM shares a transmission resource in time; frequency-division multiplexing separates channels by frequency.

questions.prompt: What is a core reason cellular systems use multiple coverage cells?
choices: Reuse radio resources across an area with interference management
Make every phone a wired landline
Require all calls to use a single global channel
questions.explanation: Cellular architecture divides coverage and coordinates radio resources; detailed implementation varies by generation.

questions.prompt: Half-duplex two-way radio generally allows which behavior?
choices: Either party can transmit, but not both simultaneously on the shared channel.
Both directions always transmit simultaneously on one undivided channel.
Only text messages can be sent.
questions.explanation: Half-duplex supports two directions with turn-taking; full-duplex permits simultaneous two-way communication.
